Manuscript submitted to ACM 1 arXiv:2311.16863v3  [cs.LG]  15 Oct 2024ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil Luccioni et al 1 INTRODUCTION Understanding the environmental impacts of different industries is an important first step towards developing effective strategies to mitigate those impacts. For newer industries such as information and communication technologies (ICT) of which Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are considered to be a part of, more work is needed to understand the extent of their environmental impacts and the factors that influence it. Between 2017 and 2021, the electricity used by Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, the main providers of commercially-available cloud compute, more than doubled [22]. According to the most recent figures available, global data centre electricity consumption has grown by 20-40% annually in recent years, reaching 1-1.3% of global electricity demand and contributing 1% of energy-related greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 [21]. However the contribution of the AI sector specifically towards these figures is unclear. Recent work documenting the environmental impacts of ML has focused largely on quantifying the operational energy and carbon required to perform the training phase of the ML model life cycle [12, 30, 41, 49] due to the relative ease of measuring per-model energy use for that phase and the impressive quantity of energy required to perform a single training run [ 41, 49]. Yet, other phases of the ML model life cycle, such as inference, stand to impact the environment just as much, or more, than training due to the computational resources required to deploy modern models at scale. While inference on a single example requires much less computation than that required to train the same model, inference happens far more frequently than model training — as many as billions of times a day for a model powering a popular user-facing product such as Google Translate.1 Yet, in-depth work quantifying the costs of model inference and deployment is limited and their environmental impacts, in terms of energy and carbon as well as water and mining of rare earth minerals, have yet to be estimated. According to AWS, the largest global cloud provider, inference is estimated to make up 80 to 90% of total ML cloud computing demand [2, 28], whereas a 2021 publication by Meta attributed approximately one-third of their internal end-to-end ML carbon footprint to model inference, with the remainder produced by data management, storage, and training [57]; similarly, a 2022 study from Google attributed 60% of its ML energy use to inference, compared to 40% for training [40]. Given the increasing ubiquity of AI model deployment, it is crucial to go beyond these high-level statistics to get a better idea of the energy requirements and carbon emissions of model inference for different models and tasks. In particular, looking at inference rather than training leads to drastically different conclusions when considering the multi-purpose (or “general-purpose”) aspect specifically. Training a single model for multiple tasks can indeed be more energy-efficient when considering training costs only, but these gains can easily be lost and even reversed over the course of the model’s lifetime, given how much inference is carried out when these models are deployed in user-facing applications like chat and web search. To help shed light on this issue, we perform an extensive study measuring the amount of energy required to deploy various ML models and architectures, including large language models (LLMs)- as such, our study is, to our knowledge, the first to focus solely on the inference phase of the ML model life cycle. We study 88 models across 10 tasks and 30 datasets, spanning applications in natural language and computer vision, analyzing the impact of end task, modality, model size, architecture, and learning paradigm (i.e. task-specific or multi-task/multi-purpose) on energy efficiency. We identify orders-of-magnitude differences in the amount of energy required per inference across models, modalities and tasks and shine light on an important trade-off between the benefit of multi-purpose systems, their energy cost, and ensuing carbon emissions. By painting a more detailed picture of widely varying energy requirements for ML model 1Google reported translating more than 100 billion words per day in 2016, assuming an average query length of 100 words yields an estimate of 1 billion queries to the model per day. Source: https://blog.google/products/translate/ten-years-of-google-translate/ 2Power Hungry Processing ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil inference, we hope this study can be useful for practitioners to better understand accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across tasks and models, as well as enabling better estimates, and projections and policy decisions at the sector level. 2 PREVIOUS WORK Estimating the energy and emissions of ML models has remains a relatively under-explored topic, albeit one that has been gathering traction since Strubell et al’s seminal article quantifying the energy and carbon emissions of a variety of then-large NLP models [2019]. Since then, most studies have focused on estimating the energy consumed and carbon emitted during the training phase of neural networks – this includes studies by Patterson et al. [2022, 2021], who compared different models and analyzed factors influencing their emissions. There have also been studies of specific model architectures, e.g. BLOOM [ 31] and Nour [27], which carried out in-depth analyses of the different steps in the models’ life cycle and their relative contribution towards the final quantity of carbon emissions. Given the increasing deployment of ML models in the cloud, several studies have therefore looked at cloud-specific ways to reduce the emissions of ML models such as delayed scheduling, workload elasticity and choosing the least carbon-intensive electricity available Chien et al. [6], Dodge et al. [12], Hanafy et al. [19]. Despite these empirical studies, there is currently a lack of standardized methodology for quantifying and comparing the energy consumption and carbon emissions of ML models. There are several tools that exist, such as Code Carbon [47], MLCO2 [26] and LLMCarbon [13], all of which adopt different approaches and output different results (see [ 1] for a detailed comparison). It is therefore difficult to systematically compare the carbon footprints of different models. Existing tools and studies have also largely focused on the dynamic power consumption (i.e. the electricity necessary for powering hardware) and its resulting emissions. However, there have been several proposals to also take into account the embodied emissions of ML models (i.e. the emissions that can be attributed to the manufacturing of computing equipment) into carbon emissions estimates. This has been impeded by a lack of transparency from the designers of common computing hardware such as GPUs, although recent estimates have revealed that the embodied carbon footprint of an LLM trained and deployed on Meta’s compute cluster constitutes up to 50% of its carbon footprint [57]. While the majority of existing work has been focused on ML model training given that it is a more tractable part of the model life cycle (i.e. it is most often carried out over a set period of time on a specific compute instance), model inference has started to also become the subject of scholarship [6, 11]. Luccioni et al. ’s study of BLOOM was the first of its kind to look at the specific energy costs related to deploying an LLM [ 31] and found that, over time, this can represent a significant portion of a model’s overall carbon footprint. The current study further pursues this line of work, delving deeper into the inference stage of ML models, the energy it consumes and the carbon it emits. By testing a variety of architectures on different tasks and datasets, we aim to gain a better understanding of the degree of variance that can be observed and how seemingly small user choices can result in large differences in model’s environmental impacts. 3 METHODOLOGY As stated above, our study focuses on the inference (i.e. deployment) stage in the model life cycle, aiming to address the knowledge gaps that currently exist with regards to its energy consumption and ensuing emissions. We describe how we chose the tasks, datasets and models in the sections below, and present the results of our analysis in Section 4. 3ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil Luccioni et al 3.1 Task and dataset selection As the starting point of our study, we chose 10 ML tasks from 5 different modalities:Text-to-category (text classifica- tion, token classification, extractive question answering), Text-to-text (masked language modeling, text generation, summarization), Image-to-category (image classification, object detection), Image-to-text (image captioning) and Text-to-image (image generation). These tasks were chosen because they are common in both Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision, allowing us to explore multiple modalities, and include several multimodal tasks (i.e. image captioning and image generation), allowing us to explore the nexus between several modalities as well. To test each of the tasks listed above, we chose three of the most downloaded datasets from the Hugging Face Hub. We present the tasks and their corresponding datasets in Table 1. Task Datasets Task Datasets image classification CIFAR 10 [25] CIFAR 100 [25] ImageNet 1K [45] question answering SQuAD[44] SQuAD v2 [43] SciQ [23] image captioning Visual Genome [24] RedCaps [10] COCO [29] summarization SAMSum [15] CNN-Daily Mail [20] XSum [35] image generation DiffusionDB [54] ImageReward [58] SD Prompts [46] text classification IMDB [32] Rotten Tomatoes [39] SST 2 [48] masked language modeling BookCorpus [59] C4 [42] OSCAR [37] text generation WikiText [33] BookCorpus [59] OSCAR [37] object detection Visual Genome [24] CPPE-5 [9] COCO [29] token classification ReCoRD [53] WikiANN [38] CoNLL 2003 [50] Table 1. A list of the tasks and datasets used in our study. 3.2 Models To be representative of a broad diversity of deployment use cases, we sampled 88 models, some of which were trained or finetuned specifically for the tasks that we selected, whereas others were designed to be used as zero-shot or multi-task models, to allow comparisons both for different architectures on a given task and between tasks for the same architecture. Task-specific Models. For all of the tasks listed above, we selected the 8 most popular models from the HuggingFace Hub (by number of downloads) 2 - we present the full list of model identifiers in Table 6 in the Supplementary Materials. For each model, we ran 1,000 inferences for each of the 3 datasets from the task it was trained for (listed in Table 1), using the Transformers [55] library. We ran each set of inferences 10 times to ensure statistical significance of our measurements. We set up the inferences sequentially – i.e., without batching – in order to reflect the variability of model deployment in situ , which can make it difficult to batch model inputs. 2We were obliged to discard some models, e.g. if they were trained on another language or if the specific task they were fine-tuned for was not compatible with any of the datasets selected. 4Power Hungry Processing ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil Multi-Purpose Models. In addition to the task-specific models listed above, we also selected 8 multi-purpose models to analyze on different tasks – models that were specifically trained to perform well in various different application settings. We chose 4 sequence-to-sequence models of different sizes from the Flan-T5 family [8] (base, large, xl and xxl) and 4 decoder-only models from the BLOOMz family [34]: BLOOMz-560M, BLOOMz-1B, BLOOMz-3B and BLOOMz-7B. We tested these on a subset of the tasks to allow a comparison of multi-purpose generative models with individual task-specific systems in terms of their energy consumption and emissions: question answering, text classification and summarization. We selected these three tasks because we were able to find a set of models that were capable of carrying them out with a unified model architecture (which wasn’t possible for all tasks, especially ones that involved multiple modalities.) We prompted these 8 models in a zero-shot setting that was constant across models, e.g. "Summarize the following text: [text]. Summary:" on the same 1,000 samples as the fine-tuned models, also repeating each experiment ten times to measure the significance of results. We ran all of our experiments on a node of 8 NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs hosted on Amazon Web Services, and used the Code Carbon package [47] to measure both the energy consumed and the carbon emitted during inference 3. Given that all of our experiments were run in the same compute region (AWS’sus-west-2), which is based in Oregon and has an average carbon intensity of 297.6 grams of 𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞per kWh4, this means that both the energy consumed during inference and the carbon emitted are correlated; we will therefore plot one or the other depending on which aspect of our results we are discussing. While the energy consumed during inference will remain similar for models deployed on A100 GPUs in other compute regions, the carbon emissions will vary depending on the source of energy used in the region – it is therefore helpful to report both energy and carbon separately to allow for meaningful comparisons across regions and hardware. We provide all the code used for our experiments in our GitHub repository, alongside the logs produced by Code Carbon, which not only provides the total energy consumed but also a more fine-grained breakdown by hardware component (GPU, CPU and RAM), which can be used to carry out further analyses. In total, for all of model experimentation and evaluation, we used a total of 754.66 kWh of energy and emitted 178.97 kg of 𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞. 4 RESULTS We present our results in the subsections below: in Section 4.1, we analyze the range of energy used and carbon emitted for each task for task-specific models. In Section 4.3, we carry out a comparison between model training and inference costs for models of different sizes, calculating when parity is reached. 4.1 Task-specific model analysis We start by analyzing the degree of variability in terms of the energy cost of ML models specifically trained for a variety of tasks. For context, the most carbon-intensive image generation model (stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0) generates 1,594 grams of𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞for 1,000 inferences, which is roughly the equivalent to 4.1 miles driven by an average gasoline-powered passenger vehicle [51], whereas the least carbon-intensive text generation model (distilbert-base-uncased) gener- ates as much carbon as 0.0006 miles driven by a similar vehicle, i.e. 6,833 times less. This can add up quickly when image generation models such as Dall·E and MidJourney are deployed in user-facing applications and used by millions of users globally (we discuss this point further in Section 5). The (high-level) takeaway of this analysis is that even for models specifically trained to carry out a single task, there is a large level of variation both within each task and an even larger one between tasks from different modalities. In essence, tasks that map both image and text inputs to categorical outputs are less energy- and carbon-intensive than those that generate text or images. Making these distinctions can help inform policies seeking to mitigate the environmental impacts of AI, given that it is important to be aware of this variation, which can sometimes reach several orders of magnitude. We further discuss our results and further avenues of research in the next and final section. 4.3 Comparing model training and inference costs An important trade-off for many AI practitioners and policy-makers is determining when exactly model inference costs reach parity with model training (and fine-tuning) - i.e. when does the deployment of models use as much energy as their initial training? This comparison is often hard to make because it requires the total energy cost of all steps of the ML model life cycle, which is very rarely available. Of the models that we examined in our study, neither the BLOOMz nor the Flan-T5 families of models reported the total energy used nor carbon emitted during their training in the papers describing the models. However, given that the BLOOMz models are fine-tuned versions of the original BLOOM family of models [56], we can base ourselves on the logs provided by the authors of the BLOOM carbon footprint estimation paper [31]. We can add to these numbers the energy cost of fine-tuning each model, which we were able to estimate based on the training logs provided by the authors of the BLOOMz paper [34], although we were lacking the necessary information to infer the carbon footprint 6. We discuss the importance of transparency and other important actions that members of the community can take in the next, and final, section. 5 DISCUSSION There have been limited studies regarding the energy consumption and carbon emissions of LLM inference, largely due to its distributed nature — compared to the relatively time- and location-constrained nature of training — making it difficult to make meaningful comparisons between different models and tasks. In this work, we have endeavored to keep as many parameters stable as possible, including the code, hardware, datasets, batch size and Python library. We provide all of the code that we used for our analysis as well as an interactive tool to allow users to more deeply explore the results we present here. We also highlight the main high-level takeaways of our study below: Generative tasks are more energy- and carbon-intensive compared to discriminative tasks. As shown in Figure 1, the most energy- and carbon-intensive tasks are those that generate new content: text generation, summarization, image captioning, and image generation. Tasks involving images are more energy- and carbon-intensive compared to those involving text alone. More specifically, tasks involving predicting categories (text-to-category, image-to-category) are less energy-intensive than those involving generating images (e.g. text-to-image), with those involving text between the two (see Figure 2). Decoder-only models are slightly more energy- and carbon- intensive than sequence-to-sequence models for models of a similar size and applied to the same tasks. The findings we present in Table 3, Figure 3, and Figure 6 would indicate that more computation (i.e. energy) is required for decoder-only tasks, and that this phenomenon is particularly marked for tasks with longer outputs. This observation is worth verifying for other architectures from both categories, and well as other tasks and datasets. Training remains orders of magnitude more energy- and carbon- intensive than inference. We have provided initial numbers for comparing the relative energy costs of model training, finetuning and inference for different sizes of models from the BLOOMz family, and found that the parity between training/finetuning and inference grows with model size. While the ratio is hundreds of millions of inferences for a single training, given the ubiquity of ML model deployment, this parity can be reached quickly for many popular models. Using multi-purpose models for discriminative tasks is more energy-intensive compared to task-specific models for these same tasks. This is especially the case for text classification (on IMDB, SST 2 and Rotten Tomatoes) and question answering (on SciQ, SQuAD v1 and v2), where the gap between task-specific and zero-shot models is particularly large, and less so for summarization (for CNN-Daily Mail, SamSUM and XSum). As can be seen in Table 4, the difference 13ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil Luccioni et al between multi-purpose models and task-specific models is amplified as the length of output gets longer. We find this last point to be the most compelling takeaway of our study, given the current paradigm shift away from smaller models finetuned for a specific task towards models that are meant to carry out a multitude of tasks at once, deployed to respond to a barrage of user queries in real time. This transition has been happening both in ML research since the advent of GPT-3 [ 5], which illustrated the potential for few- and zero-shot learning with language models, as well as in consumer settings, with LLMs such as GPT-4 and PaLM being deployed in user-facing products such as web search [4, 18], email, and navigation [17], where smaller, task-specific versions of models such as BERT were previously used [ 3, 16]. While it is hard to quantify the environmental impacts of this transition given the lack of transparency of technology companies regarding both the number of parameters, architecture and carbon emissions of their products, we can make a comparison based on the experiments carried out in the present study. For instance, the average emissions of a BERT-based model fine-tuned for extractive question answering (bert-large-uncased-whole-word-masking-finetuned-squad), a task akin to extractive web search, is 0.70g𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞 per 1,000 queries, which is less than 3 times that of the multi-purpose models (2.36g for Flan-T5 base and 2.34g for BLOOMz-560M). The difference is much more drastic if comparing BERT-based models for tasks such as text classification with the larger multi-purpose models: for instance bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment emits just 0.32g of 𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞per 1,000 queries, compared to 2.66g for Flan-T5-XL and 4.67g for BLOOMz-7B. For comparison, the first PaLM model, released in 2022, has 540 billion parameters [7], whereas GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters [5] 8. While we see the benefit of deploying generative zero-shot models given their ability to carry out multiple tasks, we do not see convincing evidence for the necessity of their deployment in contexts where tasks are well-defined, for instance web search and navigation, given these models’ energy requirements. Finally, the intent of our study is to set the stage for better understanding of the energy requirements and carbon emissions of the final, often overlooked, step in the ML model life cycle: model deployment. The comparison between training, finetuning and inference energy requirements carried out in Section 4.3 is, to our knowledge, the first comparison of its kind, and paves the way to a better understanding of how the different stages of an ML model’s lifecycle add up in terms of energy use. These are important data points that can help inform both our fellow AI researchers and practitioners, as well as policy-makers who are working towards estimating and regulating the environmental impacts of AI models and ICT in general. We recognize that our study is not representative of all deployment contexts and constraints – our intent is to establish a set of initial data points and to set the stage for testing and comparing other models. In fact, our study highlights many potential avenues for future research aimed towards a better understanding of the myriad factors that influence the efficiency of inference, including the choice of architecture, the usage of techniques such as distillation, the number of parameters, the choice of hardware and the numerical (i.e. floating point) precision of model parameters. While we encourage continued work analysing open-source models, we note that the growing lack of transparency in model architecture and training details makes this line of work, alongside many branches relating to fairness and accountability in machine learning, increasingly difficult to carry out. Given our findings and the increased deployment of generative, multi-purpose AI models, we hope that both ML researchers and practitioners will practice transparency regarding the nature and impacts of their models, to enable better understanding of their environmental impacts. 8The exact number of parameters of GPT-4 and PaLM 2 have not been publicly shared. 14Power Hungry Processing ACM FAccT ’24, June 3–6, 2024, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS STATEMENT The main ethical concerns that we faced in our experimentation is the sheer amount of energy needed and carbon emissions generated by our study, given that we ran each of the 88 models on 3 datasets 10 times to ensure statistical significance of our measurements. In total, for all of model experimentation and evaluation, we used a total of 754.66 kWh of energy and emitted 178.97 kg of 𝐶𝑂2𝑒𝑞. In order to reduce our impacts as much as possible, we did all up-front experimentations on smaller portions of the dataset (to reduce wasted resources). RESEARCHER POSITIONALITY STATEMENT The authors of this paper have backgrounds in theoretical and applied machine learning and work in institutions based in North America. We therefore recognize that our way of planning and running experiments is not necessarily reflective of other institutions from other regions, or the constraints faced by researchers from institutions with more limited access to compute. ADVERSE IMPACTS STATEMENT We recognize that our work can be perceived as a critique of ML deployment in general, given the analysis that we provide of its environmental impacts. This could be used as an argument to stop pursuing ML research and development, or as a way of targeting specific companies or organizations. Our intention, however, is to shed additional light on the environmental impacts of ML, in order to help model developers and researchers make more informed choices as a function of their environmental footprint or energy usage. new_method.method:
Open Problems: Most existing accelerators for discrete diffusion models eliminate EITHER sampling steps (e.g.
DPM-Solver, distillation) OR expensive network passes inside each step (e.g.
Encoder propagation, DeepCache, ASE).  When the step budget is already very
small (≤8) the quality of coarse-time solvers drops sharply, and the
in-network shortcuts that reuse features become ineffective because adjacent
time-steps are no longer similar.  A key unsolved problem therefore is:

How can we keep image quality at extreme low-step regimes (3-8 steps) **and**
reduce the FLOPs per step, without retraining the whole UNet or relying on
heavy teacher-student distillation?  Solving this would make near-real-time
high-resolution diffusion practical on edge devices and unlock new latency-
constrained applications.
Methods: We propose "LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp)": a plug-in module that (1) learns a
lightweight, low-rank adapter that linearly extrapolates UNet *features* in
time, and (2) warps the solver’s time-grid so that the expensive full UNet is
invoked only at information-rich key instants.

1. Key-step discovery (Time-Warp)
   • Run one dry pass of any ODE/SDE solver (e.g. DDIM-40) on a batch of
     latents and compute the per-layer feature change ΔFℓ(t)=‖Fℓ(t)−Fℓ(t−1)‖.
   • Select K key steps by maximizing overall ΔF across layers with a greedy
     sub-modular criterion (covers early noise as well as late detail).
   • Non-key steps will be approximated rather than fully recomputed.

2. Low-Rank Propagation (LoRA-Prop)
   • At every encoder/decoder block we freeze the original weights and append a
     rank-r (r≪C) LoRA adapter W_aW_b that is trained **once** for the given
     base model on a small image set (≤10 k images, 1 GPU-day).
   • Training objective:
        min ‖ F̂ℓ(t) − Fℓ(t) ‖₂ where
        F̂ℓ(t)=Fℓ(t′)+LoRAℓ(Fℓ(t′),Δt) ,   t′ = nearest previous key-step
     The adapter therefore predicts the feature at t from the cached feature at
     t′ using only a rank-r projection and a time-embedding Δt.
   • Because adapters are tiny (≤1 % parameters) the extra forward cost at
     non-key steps is negligible (two 1×1 GEMMs) and can run in INT8.
   • The scheme is **model-agnostic** (UNet, DiT, SDXL) and does not alter the
     original weights, preserving existing checkpoints and LoRA LyCORIS stacks.

3. Hybrid solver
   • A standard fast solver (e.g. DPM-Solver++/UniPC) is executed on the warped
     time-grid.  For key steps we call the full UNet; for skipped steps we use
     LoRA-Prop to propagate features layer-wise and run *only* the inexpensive
     mid-block+output layers (≈10 % of FLOPs).

Novelty v.s. prior work
   • Unlike Encoder-propagation, features are *extrapolated* rather than simply
     reused, keeping fidelity when steps are far apart.
   • Unlike distillation, we fine-tune only rank-r adapters (≲5 M params) and
     retain the original generative behaviour.
   • Combines step-reduction and per-step FLOP reduction synergistically.
Experimental Setup: Models
  • Stable Diffusion v1.5 (512²) latent UNet.
  • Diag.
    DiT-XL-2 (256²) latent model.
  • ADM-256 pixel UNet.
Datasets
  • COCO-30k prompts & validation images.
  • ImageNet-50k class-conditional set.
Baselines
  1. DPM-Solver++ (8 & 4 steps)
  2. FasterDiffusion (encoder propagation)
  3. AdaptiveDiffusion (step skipping)
  4. Moment-Matching distillation (8-step student)
Metrics
  • FID/IS (image quality)
  • CLIPScore/ImageReward (text alignment)
  • Throughput (it/s) & GFLOPs / image
  • Peak memory and mobile latency (iPhone 14 Pro A16)
  • Robustness: quality drop w.r.t. guidance scale ∈[1,15] and prompt length.
Ablations
  • Rank r ∈{4,8,16}
  • Number of key steps K ∈{2,3,4} for total NFEs 3-8.
  • Effect of INT8 vs FP16 adapters.
  • Time-grid selection strategy (greedy vs uniform).
Training cost reporting.
Implementation
  • PyTorch; adapters injected via PEFT-style API; ONNX export for mobile.
Result: Expected
  • At 4 sampling steps LoRA-Prop attains FID within +0.3 of 20-step DDIM and
    ≈1.0 better than DPM-Solver++-4.
  • Throughput improves 1.8-2.3× over FasterDiffusion and >4× over vanilla
    DPM-Solver++-4 on A100; mobile latency <1100 ms for 512×512 generation.
  • Quality remains stable across guidance scales up to 12, unlike encoder
    caching which blurs textures.
  • Parameter overhead <1 % and no additional VRAM during training.
  • Generalises: the same adapters plugged into DreamBooth-finetuned checkpoints
    degrade FID by <0.5 without retraining.
Conclusion: LoRA-Prop (+Time-Warp) demonstrates that a tiny, once-trained set of low-rank
adapters can *predict* intermediate UNet features, enabling both drastic step
reduction and per-step FLOP savings.  This fills the long-standing gap where
existing accelerators fail at extreme low-step regimes or incur full UNet
computations.

Academically, the work bridges numerical ODE solvers with neural feature
prediction, opening a principled way to trade compute for linear feature
extrapolation.  Practically, it delivers sub-second 512² text-to-image
generation on flagship phones **without** retraining huge models, making
high-fidelity diffusion viable for AR/creative apps.  Future work includes
extending the adapter prediction to video diffusion (temporal LoRA-Prop) and
exploring theoretical error bounds of feature extrapolation along diffusion
trajectories.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Below are three concrete, Python-feasible experimental plans that directly address the prior consistency issues and validate LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp) from quality, ablation, and systems perspectives. Each plan includes datasets/models/baselines, protocols for statistical rigor, bug fixes, and reproducibility provisions.

Experiment 1: End-to-end quality and statistical validation (H1/H2/H4)
Objective
- Validate that LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp) matches or improves image quality at extreme low NFE (3–8) compared to strong baselines while maintaining text alignment. Provide statistical support and ensure reproducibility.

Models and datasets
- Text-to-image: Stable Diffusion v1.5 (512×512) with COCO 2014 val5k prompts and real images for FID/CLIPScore.
- Class-conditional: DiT-XL/2 (256×256) with ImageNet-1k validation (50k) for FID/IS.
- Optional third: ADM-256 for completeness and cross-architecture confirmation (run on a 10k ImageNet subset for compute management).

Methods compared (identical time-grids, latents, guidance, seeds)
- LoRA-Prop + Time-Warp (this work): K ∈ {2,3,4} key steps; overall NFE ∈ {3,4,6,8}. Solver: UniPC and DPM-Solver++ variants on warped grid.
- Baselines (non-LoRA): DPM-Solver++ (matching NFEs), UniPC (matching NFEs), AdaptiveDiffusion, FasterDiffusion (encoder propagation), 8-step distilled student (public checkpoint or reproduced per repo).
- Controls: Full 20-step DDIM and 50-step PNDM as upper quality references.

Sampling grid and controls
- CFG ∈ {3,5,7,12}; NFE ∈ {3,4,6,8} → full factorial across methods.
- Use identical Gaussian latents per prompt/class and per seed across all methods; same time-grid per NFE for every method. For Time-Warp, fix K and warped times once per model/dataset using a disjoint dry batch.
- Seeds: ≥3 (e.g., 11, 23, 47). Assess within-seed paired comparisons.

Metrics (and correctness)
- COCO: FID (w.r.t. COCO 2014 val set; exact image list documented), CLIPScore (ViT-L/14), ImageReward; report per-prompt CLIPScore/ImageReward.
- ImageNet: FID/IS (torch-fidelity with default Inception). Verify ImageNet val reference set is correctly loaded; log SHA256 of file list.
- Robustness curves: FID and CLIPScore vs CFG for NFE ∈ {4,6}; also vs prompt length buckets (<10, 10–30, >30 tokens) using COCO captions.

Statistics and reporting
- For each (dataset, NFE, CFG): report mean metric with 95% bootstrap CI (10k paired bootstrap resamples over prompts/classes, stratified by seed). For FID/IS use torch-fidelity; for CLIPScore/ImageReward compute per-prompt, then bootstrap.
- Hypothesis testing: paired t-test vs best non-LoRA baseline per NFE, Holm–Bonferroni corrected across CFGs; report Cohen’s d and p-values. Additionally report nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank as a robustness check.
- Monotonicity check (H4): verify FID(NFE=8) ≤ FID(6) ≤ FID(4) ≤ FID(3) with overlapping 95% CIs or significant monotone trend (Kendall’s tau with p<0.05) for LoRA-Prop and baselines on both datasets.

Implementation notes (Python-feasible)
- Frameworks: diffusers, timm/torchmetrics, torch-fidelity, ImageReward pip package, OpenCLIP for CLIPScore.
- Data hygiene: Store and release exact file lists for COCO-val and ImageNet-val, resize/crop policy (512 square center-crop for SD1.5; 256 center-crop for DiT-XL/2), and tokenizer config. Log time-grids and key-step indices.
- Reproducibility: Save run-level CSV (prompt_id, seed, latent_hash, scheduler, NFE, CFG, method, time_grid_hash, key_steps, metric values) and a sqlite summary. Archive environment.yml, Git commit, CUDA/cuDNN versions.

Acceptance criteria
- At NFE=4 on COCO: LoRA-Prop FID within +0.3 of 20-step DDIM and ≥1.0 better than the best non-LoRA baseline (DPM-Solver++/UniPC/Adaptive/FasterDiffusion) with p<0.01 and |d|≥0.3.
- CLIPScore/ImageReward not significantly worse (p≥0.05) than best non-LoRA baseline at same NFE.
- Monotone FID trend vs NFE holds with significant Kendall’s tau or overlapping CIs.
- Report at least three seeds; CIs included.

Addresses prior issues
- Adds statistical support, real datasets/models, baselines at matched NFEs/CFG, multi-seed variance, monotonicity, and data hygiene.


Experiment 2: Mechanism, ablations, and bug fixes (ΔF/keys, epsilon error, ranks, INT8) (H2/H4)
Objective
- Demonstrate why LoRA-Prop works and where it helps most. Validate Time-Warp key selection, feature extrapolation quality, and robustness across ranks. Fix the previously observed evaluation bug (zero MSE).

Setups
- Models: SD1.5 (512) and DiT-XL/2 (256).
- Datasets: COCO val5k prompts; ImageNet val 50k (or 10k subset for ablation speed, but report which).

Ablations
- Key-step selection: Time-Warp (greedy submodular on ΔF across layers) vs uniform and front-loaded schedules for identical K and NFE.
- Rank r ∈ {4,8,16}; K ∈ {2,3,4}; INT8 vs FP16 adapters.
- Cache-only vs LoRA-Prop (both use identical key-steps and time-grids).

Mechanism diagnostics
- ΔF heatmaps: For dry runs (e.g., DDIM-40 on 1k latents), compute ΔF_l(t)=||F_l(t)-F_l(t-1)||₂ normalized per layer. Visualize layer-time maps and overlay selected key steps. Release the arrays as .npz for reproducibility.
- Per-step epsilon and feature errors: For each non-key step t with nearest previous key-step t′, compute MSE/LPIPS between: (a) predicted features F̂_l(t) vs ground truth F_l(t); (b) UNet epsilon prediction ε̂(t) vs ε(t). Also PSNR/LPIPS on final images vs full 20-step DDIM as teacher.

Bug fix: preventing zero MSE artifact
- Correct reference storage and step alignment:
  - At step t, before any in-place ops, clone and detach ground-truth tensors: gt_eps[t] = eps_t.detach().cpu(); gt_feat[l][t] = F_l(t).detach().cpu().
  - Compute previous-step baselines with explicit indices: prev_eps = gt_eps[t-1]; never reuse the same tensor reference.
  - Unit test: assert MSE(prev_eps, gt_eps[t]) > 0 for at least 95% of steps on a random batch; if not, flag.
- Add regression test that intentionally shuffles time indices; MSE should increase.

Quality endpoints and stats
- End-to-end: FID/CLIPScore/ImageReward for LoRA-Prop vs cache-only vs non-LoRA baselines at NFE ∈ {4,6} on COCO; FID/IS on ImageNet. 95% CIs, paired tests, Cohen’s d.
- Time-Warp validation: At NFE=4 and K fixed, LoRA-Prop with Time-Warp must significantly outperform uniform/front-loaded key schedules on FID (paired tests, Holm–Bonferroni, p<0.01). Release ΔF maps and key indices.
- Monotonicity: Confirm FID decreases with NFE for each rank r; check trend significance.
- INT8 adapters: Compare FP16 vs INT8 on adapters only at NFE ∈ {4,6}; report ΔFID, ΔCLIPScore with 95% CIs. Require ΔFID ≤ 0.3 and no significant CLIPScore drop (p≥0.05).

Implementation details (Python-feasible)
- Feature taps: Hook UNet/DiT blocks using register_forward_hook; ensure eval mode and no dropout. Cache F_l(t′) in a dict keyed by (layer_id, step_index).
- LoRA injection: PEFT-style adapters per block; time-embedding for Δt via sinusoidal or learned MLP. Train adapters for ≤10k images (one GPU-day). Use AMP.
- INT8: Quantize adapters only with bitsandbytes (Linear8bitLt) on GPU; for CPU/mobile, use dynamic quantization on the adapter Linear layers and export QLinear ops in ONNX.
- Metrics: LPIPS via lpips package, PSNR via torchmetrics.

Acceptance criteria
- LoRA-Prop significantly better than cache-only on feature/epsilon errors and final FID at NFE {4,6} (p<0.01).
- Time-Warp statistically better than uniform/front-loaded at NFE=4 (p<0.01) with visible ΔF alignment.
- INT8 passes ΔFID ≤ 0.3 with non-significant CLIPScore drop.
- No zero-MSE artifacts in any diagnostic; unit tests pass.

Addresses prior issues
- Adds baselines/controls and ablations; fixes evaluation bug; validates Time-Warp; demonstrates monotonicity; tests INT8 quality robustness.


Experiment 3: Systems and deployment validation (GFLOPs, throughput, ONNX/CoreML/mobile) (H8–H10)
Objective
- Substantiate compute and latency claims, validate analytic vs measured GFLOPs, and verify deployment parity and speedups on GPU and mobile.

Hardware and runtimes
- Server: A100 80GB, CUDA 12+, PyTorch 2.x with torch.compile off (and on, reported separately). Batch size 1 and 4; mixed precision.
- Mobile: iPhone 14 Pro (A16), iOS 17+, CoreML and/or ONNXRuntime Mobile. Measure cold and warm latencies.

GFLOPs, memory, and throughput
- Analytic GFLOPs/image: fvcore FlopCountAnalysis on UNet/DiT with inputs of correct shapes for key and non-key steps. Sum across steps for given NFE and method; report per-layer shares to show mid-block-only path.
- Measured FLOPs/time: torch.profiler with kineto; measure FLOPs where supported and wall-time per step. Compare analytic vs measured FLOPs; require agreement within 5%.
- Throughput: images/sec on A100 for NFE ∈ {4,6,8}, CFG ∈ {5,7,12}. Compare LoRA-Prop+Time-Warp vs DPM-Solver++/UniPC/FasterDiffusion and distilled-8. Report mean ± std over 30 runs.
- Peak memory: torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated across methods.

INT8 on server
- Adapters-only INT8 using bitsandbytes; measure speedup and ΔFID/CLIPScore at NFE {4,6}. Report 95% CIs; require ΔFID ≤ 0.3.

Mobile/ONNX/CoreML pipeline
- Export path:
  - Remove Python assert in forward; move shape checks outside traced graph or use torch._assert. Freeze control-flow where possible.
  - Export two models: (A) full UNet key-step subgraph; (B) non-key-step light subgraph (mid-block + output + LoRA adapters). Use ONNX opset ≥17 with QLinear ops for INT8 adapters, or CoreML neural network with weight quantization to 8-bit.
- Parity checks:
  - On a held-out batch (128 images), compute PyTorch vs ONNX/CoreML outputs at non-key steps: PSNR/MAE on features and ε; require PSNR ≥ 40 dB and MAE ≤ 1e-3. Also compare final images PSNR/LPIPS.
- On-device latency
  - Build a simple iOS harness that orchestrates key/non-key steps and measures end-to-end time for 512×512, CFG {5,7}, NFE {4,6}. Report median and p95 across 30 runs (cold/warm). Target <1100 ms for 512×512 at NFE=4.

Reproducibility and logging
- Provide per-run CSV with timing, GFLOPs (analytic and measured), memory, device info. Save profiler traces (Chrome trace JSON) and model hashes.

Acceptance criteria
- ≥55% GFLOPs reduction at NFE=4 vs DPM-Solver++-4; analytic vs measured within 5%.
- Throughput 1.8–2.3× over FasterDiffusion and >4× over vanilla DPM-Solver++-4 on A100 for batch=1.
- INT8 adapters deliver measurable speedup with ΔFID ≤ 0.3 and non-significant CLIPScore change.
- Mobile: <1100 ms median latency at 512×512, NFE=4; parity PSNR/LPIPS within thresholds.

Addresses prior issues
- Substantiates systems claims with GFLOPs accounting, throughput, INT8 quality delta, and mobile latency; fixes ONNX export assertion issue; adds parity checks.


Shared training protocol for LoRA-Prop adapters (for completeness)
- Data: 10k images from LAION-Aesthetics or COCO train split with text prompts; augment with random crops/resizes matching model resolution; use SD1.5 text embeddings for conditioning when applicable.
- Loss: L2 on features and ε at non-key steps using cached F_l(t′) and Δt; auxiliary LPIPS on decoded images for stability; optimizer AdamW, lr=1e-4, wd=1e-4; cosine decay; 1 GPU-day A100; rank r ∈ {4,8,16}. Freeze base weights; train adapters only. Save adapter checkpoints and training logs.

Data/implementation hygiene checklist (applies to all experiments)
- Correct FID references: use official COCO 2014 val images (5k) and ImageNet val (50k); release file lists and SHA256. Verify torch-fidelity sees the correct references (log counts and a few hashes).
- Identical latents/time-grids across methods; log seeds and latent hashes.
- Remove in-graph asserts before ONNX tracing; use torch._assert or pre-export checks.
- Release time-grids, key-step indices, adapter ranks, environment hashes, and all per-run CSV/sqlite logs.

Generalization check (attach to Experiment 1 or 2)
- Plug trained adapters into 5 DreamBooth-finetuned SD1.5 checkpoints without retraining. Evaluate ΔFID and CLIPScore with CIs at NFE {4,6}. Acceptance: ΔFID ≤ 0.5 and non-significant CLIPScore change.

If executed, these three plans jointly provide statistically grounded quality evidence, strong ablations/controls (including bug fixes), and comprehensive systems validation on both server and mobile targets.

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 1 ─ End-to-End Quality + Statistical Validation (H1/H2/H4)
================================================================================
Goal
  • Show that LoRA-Prop (+Time-Warp) keeps or improves quality at NFE ≤8 while
    lowering compute, and that quality improves monotonically with NFE.

Hardware & env
  • 8×A100-80GB, CUDA-12.2, PyTorch-2.1, torch-compile OFF (quality runs) and ON
    (separate speed runs).  Ubuntu-22.04, Python-3.10, diffusers-0.23.
  • Fixed env.yml committed to repo; hash logged per run.

1) Models / checkpoints
  SD-1.5 (CompVis 768-v1) … 512² text-cond.
  DiT-XL/2 (OpenAI public ckpt) … 256² class-cond.
  (Optional) ADM-256 (OpenAI) … 256² class-cond.

2) Datasets
  COCO-2014 val5k prompts + images – FID/CLIPScore/ImageReward.
  ImageNet-1k val (all 50 000 imgs) – FID/IS.
  SHA-256 of every file list dumped to csv (see data/hashlists/).

3) Methods compared (identical latents/time-grids)
  M0 20-step DDIM              (oracle upper-bound)
  M1 50-step PNDM              (slow upper-bound)
  M2 DPM-Solver++-{3,4,6,8}
  M3 UniPC-{3,4,6,8}
  M4 FasterDiffusion encoder-prop (FD-{3,4,6,8})
  M5 AdaptiveDiffusion skip     (ADA-{3,4,6,8})
  M6 Distilled-8-step student   (D8)
  M7 LoRA-Prop-Time-Warp (ours) with K={2,3,4} → NFE={3,4,6,8}

4) Factor grid
  NFE∈{3,4,6,8} × CFG∈{3,5,7,12} × seed∈{11,23,47}.  3(seeds)×4(NFE)×4(CFG)=48
  configs per method, ⇒ ~15 M images total (split across 8 GPUs).

5) Sampling control
  • Swiss-army scheduler: for each (method, NFE) derive the same base times τ.
    For LoRA-Prop, warp those τ → τ* using K key-steps determined once on a
    disjoint ‘dry’ batch (512 latents) and cached to json.
  • latents: torch.randn(seed) and stored (.npz).  Re-used verbatim.

6) Metrics & statistics
  a) FID/IS – torch-fidelity 0.3.0 (Inception-v3 fixed weight).  10 000 paired
     bootstrap resamples over prompts/classes (seed-stratified) → 95 % CI.
  b) CLIPScore – open_clip ViT-L/14.  Per prompt score then bootstrap.
  c) ImageReward – imagen-rewards 0.0.3.  Same procedure.
  d) Hypothesis tests – SciPy 1.11:
       • Paired t-test ours vs best non-LoRA baseline @ same (NFE,CFG).
       • Wilcoxon signed-rank as robustness check.
       • Holm-Bonferroni correction across 4 CFGs.
       • Effect size Cohen’s d.
  e) Monotonicity – Kendall’s τ trend test (τ>0 & p<0.05) + CI ordering check.

7) Expected acceptance
  • At NFE=4 (COCO) – FID(ours) ≤ FID(DDIM-20)+0.3 AND better than any baseline
    by ≥1.0 with p<0.01, |d|≥0.3.  CLIP & ImageReward not worse (p≥0.05).

8) Python skeleton (abbrev.)
"""python
import torch, json, itertools, numpy as np
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline
from torch_fidelity import calculate_metrics
from open_clip import get_tokenizer, create_model_and_transforms
from imagereward import ImageReward
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

###############################
# 1. Load latents & time grid #
###############################
latents = torch.load('latents_seed23.pt').to('cuda')
with open('time_grid_4.json') as f:
    base_times = torch.tensor(json.load(f)).to('cuda')
warp = torch.tensor(json.load(open('warp_sd15_K3.json'))).to('cuda')  # ours

###################
# 2. Run sampling #
###################
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
                                              torch_dtype=torch.float16).to('cuda')
# inject LoRA-Prop adapters if method=="ours"...
from lora_prop import inject_adapters
pipe = inject_adapters(pipe, ckpt='adapters/sd15_r8.pt', int8=False)

imgs = pipe(prompt=batch_prompts,
            latents=latents,
            num_inference_steps=4,
            guidance_scale=7,
            time_grid=warp if method=="ours" else base_times,
            key_steps=[0,1,3] if method=="ours" else None).images
#################
# 3. Save & log #
#################
for i,(img,prompt) in enumerate(zip(imgs,batch_prompts)):
    img.save(f'outputs/{run_id}/{i}.png')
# metrics aggregated later via torch-fidelity + bootstrap utils
"""

9) Post-processing & plots
  • A single analyse.py script loads CSVs → pandas → seaborn line-plots FID vs
    NFE; shaded 95 % CI; also bar-plot of effect sizes.  Stored as pdf/png.
  • All raw metric files zipped and uploaded (commit hash in filename).

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 2 ─ Mechanism / Ablation / Bug-Fix (H2/H4)
================================================================================
Purpose
  • Explain *why* LoRA-Prop works: show ΔF key selection, feature extrapolation
    accuracy, rank/INT8 effects, and verify no zero-MSE bug.

1) Set-up
  • Same HW + env as Exp-1.
  • Models: SD-1.5 & DiT-XL/2.  Datasets: COCO-val5k & ImageNet-val10k.

2) Ablation matrix (≈100 runs)
  a) Key schedule ∈ {Time-Warp, Uniform, Front-loaded}
  b) Rank r ∈ {4,8,16}
  c) Adapter dtype ∈ {FP16, INT8-only}
  d) Cache-only vs LoRA-Prop
  e) NFE ∈ {4,6}

3) Diagnostics
  • ΔF heatmap – register_forward_hook on every ResBlock output during a
    DDIM-40 dry run (512 latents).  Save ΔF_l(t) ndarray, visualise via pyplot
    (layer on y-axis, step on x).  Over-plot K selected key-steps.
  • Per-step errors – for each non-key step t:
      MSE_ε  = mse( ε̂(t), ε(t) )
      MSE_Fl = mse( F̂_l(t), F_l(t) ) per layer + LPIPS image space.
    Log to TensorBoard + csv.
  • Unit-test for bug-fix – in tests/test_mse.py:
"""python
mse = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss
eps_prev = torch.randn(4,4)
eps_cur  = torch.randn(4,4)
assert not torch.allclose(eps_prev, eps_cur)  # should fail if zero-bug present
"""

4) Evaluation metrics & stats

5) Expected findings
  a) ΔF peaks cluster at early + late diffusion times; Time-Warp chooses them.
  b) LoRA-Prop reduces feature-MSE vs cache-only by ≥35 % (p<1e-4).
  c) Rank-8 balances quality & size; rank-4 slightly worse FID+0.4; rank-16 no
     further gain.
  d) INT8 (adapters-only) ΔFID ≤0.2, non-sig CLIP diff.

6) Minimal code snippets
"""python

activations = {}

# visualise
import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
mat = np.stack([deltaF[k] for k in sorted(deltaF)],axis=0)
sns.heatmap(mat, vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(mat,95))
plt.savefig('deltaF_heatmap.png')
"""

EXPERIMENT 3 ─ Systems / Deployment Validation (H8–H10)
================================================================================
Objective
  • Prove the compute & latency claims on GPU and iPhone; cross-check analytic

1) Hardware & runtimes

2) GFLOPs accounting

EXPECTED IMPACT
================================================================================
If all acceptance criteria are met, LoRA-Prop (+Time-Warp) will be the first
method that:
  • Retains near-teacher FID/CLIPScore at 4 steps *and* halves per-step FLOPs.
  • Realises >2× throughput over best encoder-reuse baseline on A100.
  • Runs under 1.1 s on an iPhone 14 Pro for 512² generation without teacher
    distillation or full-UNet INT8 quantisation.
  • Generalises to DreamBooth-fine-tunes with <0.5 FID loss.

The three experiments above collectively fix the statistical, baseline,
reproducibility, systems, and bug issues highlighted in the prior review while
remaining entirely feasible in standard PyTorch tooling.

LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp) Experimental Suite

- Includes robust logging, reproducibility, identical latents/time-grids, bootstrap CIs, paired tests, effect sizes, and trend checks.
- Provides ONNX export, analytic vs measured GFLOPs, INT8 adapters (if bitsandbytes available), and parity checks.
- Saves all plots as PDF with the specified filename scheme.
- Includes a quick test (quick_test()) that runs fast with a toy UNet to verify functionality without large models/datasets.

Note: Full experiments with SD1.5/DiT and large datasets require appropriate hardware and datasets.
"""

import os
import io

import gc
import sys
import csv

import hashlib

from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict

import numpy as np
import torch

def set_seed(seed: int):

    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True

def tensor_sha256(x: torch.Tensor) -> str:
    with torch.no_grad():
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        h.update(x.detach().cpu().numpy().tobytes())
        return h.hexdigest()


def json_dump(obj: Any, path: str):

# ----------------------------
# Stats: Bootstrap, tests, CIs

from scipy import stats


def bootstrap_ci(values: np.ndarray, n_boot: int = 10000, ci: float = 0.95, seed: int = 123) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    values = np.asarray(values)
    if values.ndim == 0:
        values = values[None]
    n = len(values)
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(n_boot, n))
    samples = values[idx].mean(axis=1)
    low = np.quantile(samples, (1-ci)/2)
    high = np.quantile(samples, 1-(1-ci)/2)
    return float(low), float(high)


def paired_ttest_and_effect(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> Dict[str, float]:
    # paired t-test (a vs b) and Cohen's d
    a = np.asarray(a)
    b = np.asarray(b)
    diff = a - b
    t, p = stats.ttest_rel(a, b, nan_policy='omit')
    d = diff.mean() / (diff.std(ddof=1) + 1e-12)
    return {"t": float(t), "p": float(p), "cohens_d": float(d)}


def holm_bonferroni(pvals: List[float], alpha: float = 0.05) -> List[bool]:
    # returns list of rejections after Holm-Bonferroni correction
    m = len(pvals)
    order = np.argsort(pvals)
    rejections = [False]*m
    for k, idx in enumerate(order):
        threshold = alpha / (m - k)
        if pvals[idx] <= threshold:
            rejections[idx] = True
        else:
            # once a null is not rejected, all larger p-values are not rejected
            break
    return rejections


def kendall_tau_trend(xs: List[float], ys: List[float]) -> Dict[str, float]:
    # Tests monotone decreasing trend of FID vs NFE
    tau, p = stats.kendalltau(xs, ys)
    return {"tau": float(tau), "p": float(p)}

# ----------------------------
# LoRA-Prop Components
# ----------------------------
class SinusoidalTimeEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim: int = 128):
        super().__init__()
        self.dim = dim
        self.proj = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(dim, dim), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(dim, dim)
        )

    def forward(self, delta_t: torch.Tensor):  # delta_t in [0,1] (normalized)
        half = self.dim // 2
        device = delta_t.device
        freqs = torch.exp(
            torch.linspace(math.log(1e-4), 0, steps=half, device=device)
        )
        angles = delta_t[:, None] * freqs[None, :] * 2 * math.pi
        emb = torch.cat([torch.sin(angles), torch.cos(angles)], dim=-1)
        if emb.shape[-1] < self.dim:
            emb = F.pad(emb, (0, self.dim - emb.shape[-1]))
        return self.proj(emb)


class LoRAAdapter(nn.Module):
    """Rank-r low-rank adapter with time embedding modulation for feature propagation.
    Assumes input features are (B, C, H, W). Applies 1x1 conv as two rank-r GEMMs.
    """
    def __init__(self, channels: int, rank: int = 8, time_dim: int = 128):
        super().__init__()
        self.rank = rank
        self.channels = channels
        self.down = nn.Conv2d(channels, rank, kernel_size=1, bias=False)
        self.up = nn.Conv2d(rank, channels, kernel_size=1, bias=False)
        self.time_emb = SinusoidalTimeEmbedding(time_dim)
        self.mod = nn.Linear(time_dim, rank)
        # Initialize near-zero to preserve base behavior
        nn.init.zeros_(self.down.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.mod.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.mod.bias)

    def forward(self, feat_prev: torch.Tensor, delta_t: torch.Tensor):
        B, C, H, W = feat_prev.shape
        t_emb = self.time_emb(delta_t)  # (B, time_dim)
        scale = self.mod(t_emb).view(B, self.rank, 1, 1)
        z = self.down(feat_prev)
        z = z * (1 + scale)
        out = self.up(z)
        return feat_prev + out  # residual prediction


class AdapterBank(nn.Module):
    """Holds per-layer adapters keyed by a string layer_id."""
    def __init__(self, layer_channels: Dict[str, int], rank: int = 8):
        super().__init__()
        self.adapters = nn.ModuleDict({k: LoRAAdapter(c, rank=rank) for k, c in layer_channels.items()})

    def forward(self, layer_id: str, feat_prev: torch.Tensor, delta_t: torch.Tensor):
        return self.adapters[layer_id](feat_prev, delta_t)


# ----------------------------
# Time-Warp Key-Step Discovery
# ----------------------------
@dataclass
class KeyStepConfig:
    n_dry_steps: int = 40
    top_k: int = 3
    stratify_bins: int = 4  # to encourage coverage over time


def compute_deltaF_heatmap(get_features_fn, n_steps: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, List[str]]:
    """Runs get_features_fn(step_index:int)->Dict[layer_id, torch.Tensor] for t=0..n_steps-1
    Returns matrix (n_layers, n_steps) of L2 norms of per-step changes and layer_ids order.
    """
    feats_prev: Dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {}
    layer_ids: List[str] = []
    deltas: Dict[str, List[float]] = {}
    for t in range(n_steps):
        feats = get_features_fn(t)
        if not layer_ids:
            layer_ids = sorted(list(feats.keys()))
            for k in layer_ids:
                deltas[k] = []
        if t > 0:
            for k in layer_ids:
                a = feats[k]
                b = feats_prev[k]
                delta = (a - b).float().pow(2).sum().sqrt().item()
                deltas[k].append(delta)
        feats_prev = {k: v.detach().cpu() for k, v in feats.items()}
    # build matrix (layers x (n_steps-1))
    mat = np.stack([deltas[k] for k in layer_ids], axis=0)
    return mat, layer_ids


def greedy_timewarp_key_selection(deltaF: np.ndarray, K: int, stratify_bins: int = 4) -> List[int]:
    """Greedy selection of K key steps based on summed ΔF across layers with time stratification.
    deltaF: (L, T-1) for steps 1..T-1. We'll pick indices in 1..T-1 inclusive.
    """
    L, Tm1 = deltaF.shape
    scores = deltaF.sum(axis=0)  # (T-1)
    # bin indices to encourage spread
    bins = np.digitize(np.arange(Tm1), np.linspace(0, Tm1, stratify_bins+1)[1:-1])
    selected = []
    used_bins = set()
    # First pass: pick top across different bins
    for _ in range(min(K, stratify_bins)):
        mask = np.ones_like(scores, dtype=bool)
        for b in used_bins:
            mask &= (bins != b)
        idx = np.argmax(np.where(mask, scores, -np.inf))
        if not np.isfinite(scores[idx]):
            break
        selected.append(int(idx+1))
        used_bins.add(int(bins[idx]))
    # Fill remaining with highest remaining scores and distance diversity
    while len(selected) < K:
        penalty = np.zeros_like(scores)
        for s in selected:
            penalty += 0.1 / (np.abs(np.arange(Tm1) - (s-1)) + 1)
        idx = np.argmax(scores - penalty)
        if int(idx+1) not in selected:
            selected.append(int(idx+1))
        else:
            # fallback to next best
            order = np.argsort(-(scores - penalty))
            for j in order:
                if int(j+1) not in selected:
                    selected.append(int(j+1))
                    break
        if len(selected) >= K:
            break
    selected = sorted(selected)
    return selected


# ----------------------------------------
# Diffusers UNet wrapper for non-key steps
# ----------------------------------------
class UNetSkipper(nn.Module):
    """
    Wraps a diffusers UNet2DConditionModel to:
    - Record down-block features at key steps (via hooks) and cache them per step.
    - At non-key steps, propagate cached features from the nearest previous key step using LoRA adapters,
      and run only mid_block + up_blocks to compute output, skipping down_blocks.
    Notes:
    - This relies on diffusers UNet structure (down_blocks, mid_block, up_blocks) being available.
    - This is a light re-implementation of the forward pass to enable partial computation.
    """
    def __init__(self, unet, rank: int = 8, device: Optional[torch.device] = None):
        super().__init__()
        self.unet = unet
        self.device = device or next(unet.parameters()).device
        # Identify layer channel sizes from down_blocks outputs (inspect modules)
        layer_channels = {}
        for i, db in enumerate(self.unet.down_blocks):
            # try to get output conv channels from the last conv in the block
            ch = None
            for name, m in db.named_modules():
                if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d):
                    ch = m.out_channels
            if ch is None:
                ch = self.unet.config.block_out_channels[min(i, len(self.unet.config.block_out_channels)-1)]
            layer_channels[f"down_{i}"] = ch
        self.adapters = AdapterBank(layer_channels, rank=rank).to(self.device)
        self.cache: Dict[int, Dict[str, torch.Tensor]] = {}
        self.cached_eps: Dict[int, torch.Tensor] = {}
        self.delta_eps_log: Dict[int, float] = {}

    def clear_cache(self):
        self.cache.clear()
        self.cached_eps.clear()
        self.delta_eps_log.clear()

    def forward_key(self, sample, timestep, encoder_hidden_states, return_eps_only: bool = True):
        # run full unet and capture down features via forward hooks
        feats: Dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {}
        hooks = []
        def make_hook(tag):
            def hook_fn(_m, _inp, out):
                feats[tag] = out.detach()
            return hook_fn
        for i, db in enumerate(self.unet.down_blocks):
            hooks.append(db.register_forward_hook(lambda m, inp, out, i=i: feats.__setitem__(f"down_{i}", out.detach())))
        out = self.unet(sample=sample, timestep=timestep, encoder_hidden_states=encoder_hidden_states)
        for h in hooks:
            h.remove()
        eps = out.sample
        return (eps, feats) if not return_eps_only else eps

    def forward_nonkey(self, sample, timestep, encoder_hidden_states, t_prev: int, delta_t_norm: torch.Tensor):
        # Skip down_blocks: use cached and adapted features
        assert t_prev in self.cache, "No cached features for previous key step"
        cached_feats = self.cache[t_prev]
        B = sample.shape[0]
        # Time embedding reused from unet internals
        temb = None
        if hasattr(self.unet, 'time_proj') and hasattr(self.unet, 'time_embedding'):
            t = timestep if isinstance(timestep, torch.Tensor) else torch.tensor([timestep], device=sample.device).repeat(B)
            t_emb = self.unet.time_proj(t)
            temb = self.unet.time_embedding(t_emb)
        # Down path is skipped; we approximate features per layer
        prop_feats = []
        for i, db in enumerate(self.unet.down_blocks):
            layer_id = f"down_{i}"
            f_prev = cached_feats[layer_id].to(sample.device)
            # Build delta_t per batch
            dt = delta_t_norm.to(sample.device).float().view(B)
            f_hat = self.adapters(layer_id, f_prev, dt)
            prop_feats.append(f_hat)
        # Mid block uses sample; run mid and up with propagated skips
        # Re-run mid_block with current sample (cannot skip mid entirely)
        x = sample
        if temb is not None:
            x = self.unet.mid_block(x, temb=temb)
        else:
            x = self.unet.mid_block(x)
        # up_blocks expect a list of residuals from down path in reverse order
        res_samples = prop_feats
        for i, ub in enumerate(self.unet.up_blocks):
            # up_block forward signature may vary; support both with/without temb
            kwargs = {"hidden_states": x, "res_hidden_states_tuple": tuple(res_samples[-(i+1):] if i == 0 else tuple(res_samples[:-i])}
            # diffusers up_blocks often expect sample + res connections
            try:
                if temb is not None:
                    x = ub(x, res_hidden_states_tuple=tuple(res_samples), temb=temb)
                else:
                    x = ub(x, res_hidden_states_tuple=tuple(res_samples))
            except TypeError:
                # Fallback signature
                if temb is not None:
                    x = ub(hidden_states=x, res_hidden_states_tuple=tuple(res_samples), temb=temb)
                else:
                    x = ub(hidden_states=x, res_hidden_states_tuple=tuple(res_samples))
        # head
        out = self.unet.conv_norm_out(x)
        out = self.unet.conv_act(out)
        out = self.unet.conv_out(out)
        return out


# ---------------------------------------
# Sampling Orchestrator & Metrics
# ---------------------------------------
@dataclass
class RunConfig:
    model_id: str = "runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5"
    device: str = "cuda"
    precision: str = "fp16"
    seeds: Tuple[int, ...] = (11, 23, 47)
    nfe_list: Tuple[int, ...] = (3, 4, 6, 8)
    cfg_scales: Tuple[float, ...] = (3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 12.0)
    method_list: Tuple[str, ...] = ("dpmpp", "unipc", "cache_only", "ours_lora_prop")
    out_root: str = "./outputs"
    save_images: bool = True


def prepare_pipeline_and_scheduler(model_id: str, device: str = "cuda", precision: str = "fp16"):
    from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline, DPMSolverMultistepScheduler, UniPCMultistepScheduler
    torch_dtype = torch.float16 if precision == "fp16" else torch.float32
    pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype=torch_dtype)
    pipe = pipe.to(device)
    pipe.set_progress_bar_config(disable=True)
    sched_dpmpp = DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config)
    sched_unipc = UniPCMultistepScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config)
    return pipe, sched_dpmpp, sched_unipc


def get_time_grid(scheduler, num_inference_steps: int) -> List[float]:
    # Build standardized timesteps in scheduler terms
    scheduler.set_timesteps(num_inference_steps)
    return scheduler.timesteps.detach().cpu().float().tolist()


def identical_latents(pipe, batch_size: int, seed: int = 0) -> torch.Tensor:
    generator = torch.Generator(device=pipe.device).manual_seed(seed)
    latents = torch.randn((batch_size, pipe.unet.config.in_channels, pipe.unet.config.sample_size, pipe.unet.config.sample_size), generator=generator, device=pipe.device, dtype=pipe.unet.dtype)
    return latents


# Metrics wrappers

def compute_fid_is(ref_dir: str, gen_dir: str) -> Dict[str, float]:
    from torch_fidelity import calculate_metrics
    metrics = calculate_metrics(input1=ref_dir, input2=gen_dir, fid=True, isc=True, verbose=False)
    return {"fid": float(metrics.get('frechet_inception_distance', np.nan)), "is_mean": float(metrics.get('inception_score_mean', np.nan))}


def compute_clipscore(prompts: List[str], images_dir: str) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, List[str]]:
    import open_clip
    from PIL import Image
    model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms('ViT-L-14', pretrained='openai')
    model.eval()
    tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer('ViT-L-14')
    ims = []
    for i in range(len(prompts)):
        img = Image.open(os.path.join(images_dir, f"{i}.png")).convert('RGB')
        ims.append(preprocess(img))
    ims = torch.stack(ims)
    with torch.no_grad():
        txt = tokenizer(prompts)
        txt_feat = model.encode_text(txt)
        img_feat = model.encode_image(ims)
        txt_feat = txt_feat / txt_feat.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        img_feat = img_feat / img_feat.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        sims = (img_feat @ txt_feat.T).diagonal().cpu().numpy()
    return sims, [f"{i}.png" for i in range(len(prompts))]


def compute_imagereward(prompts: List[str], images_dir: str) -> np.ndarray:
    try:
        from imagereward import ImageReward
        from PIL import Image
        scorer = ImageReward()
        scores = []
        for i, p in enumerate(prompts):
            img_path = os.path.join(images_dir, f"{i}.png")
            scores.append(float(scorer.score(p, img_path)))
        return np.array(scores)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[WARN] ImageReward not available: {e}")
        return np.full((len(prompts),), np.nan)


# ----------------------------------
# Epsilon/Feature error (bug-fixed)
# ----------------------------------
class EpsFeatRecorder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.gt_eps: Dict[int, torch.Tensor] = {}
        self.feats_by_layer: Dict[str, Dict[int, torch.Tensor]] = {}

    def record_step(self, step_idx: int, eps: torch.Tensor, feats: Dict[str, torch.Tensor]):
        # Correct: clone/detach per step BEFORE any reuse; store on CPU to avoid aliasing
        self.gt_eps[step_idx] = eps.detach().clone().cpu()
        for k, v in feats.items():
            if k not in self.feats_by_layer:
                self.feats_by_layer[k] = {}
            self.feats_by_layer[k][step_idx] = v.detach().clone().cpu()

    def mse_prev_eps(self, step_idx: int) -> float:
        # Compare to previous step's epsilon (sanity; should not be zero)
        if step_idx-1 not in self.gt_eps or step_idx not in self.gt_eps:
            return float('nan')
        a = self.gt_eps[step_idx-1].float()
        b = self.gt_eps[step_idx].float()
        return float(F.mse_loss(a, b).item())


# -------------------------------------------
# Experiment 1: Quality + Statistical Rigor
# -------------------------------------------

def experiment1_quality(cfg: RunConfig, prompts: List[str], ref_images_dir: Optional[str] = None):
    print("[Exp1] Starting End-to-End Quality + Statistical Validation")
    ensure_dir(cfg.out_root)
    pipe, sched_dpmpp, sched_unipc = prepare_pipeline_and_scheduler(cfg.model_id, cfg.device, cfg.precision)

    # Precompute time-warp key steps on a dry pass (disjoint batch)
    print("[Exp1] Computing ΔF heatmap for Time-Warp key-step discovery …")
    dry_n = min(8, len(prompts))
    dry_latents = identical_latents(pipe, dry_n, seed=123)

    def dry_get_features(step_idx: int) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
        # Use DDIM-like linear time grid of length 40
        num_steps = 40
        from diffusers import DDIMScheduler
        ddim = DDIMScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config)
        ddim.set_timesteps(num_steps)
        t = ddim.timesteps[step_idx].to(pipe.device)
        # Capture down-block outputs via hooks
        feats: Dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {}
        hooks = []
        for i, db in enumerate(pipe.unet.down_blocks):
            hooks.append(db.register_forward_hook(lambda m, inp, out, i=i: feats.__setitem__(f"down_{i}", out.detach().cpu())))
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = pipe.unet(sample=dry_latents, timestep=t, encoder_hidden_states=pipe._encode_prompt(prompts[:dry_n], device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=False))
        for h in hooks:
            h.remove()
        return feats

    deltaF, layer_ids = compute_deltaF_heatmap(dry_get_features, n_steps=40)
    key_steps = greedy_timewarp_key_selection(deltaF, K=3, stratify_bins=4)
    print(f"[Exp1] Selected key steps (on DDIM-40 grid indices 1..39): {key_steps}")
    plot_heatmap(deltaF, title="ΔF Heatmap (SD1.5)", xlabel="Step", ylabel="Layer", out_pdf=os.path.join(cfg.out_root, "deltaF_heatmap_sd15_timewarp.pdf"), key_steps=key_steps)

    # Run methods and collect metrics
    all_results = []
    for seed in cfg.seeds:
        for nfe in cfg.nfe_list:
            for cfg_scale in cfg.cfg_scales:
                # identical latents and base time-grid from UniPC (for example)
                base_sched = sched_unipc
                base_sched.set_timesteps(nfe)
                base_times = base_sched.timesteps.detach().cpu().tolist()
                latents = identical_latents(pipe, len(prompts), seed)
                latent_hash = tensor_sha256(latents[0])

                for method in cfg.method_list:
                    out_dir = os.path.join(cfg.out_root, f"exp1_{method}_nfe{nfe}_cfg{int(cfg_scale)}_seed{seed}")
                    ensure_dir(out_dir)
                    print(f"[Exp1] Sampling method={method} NFE={nfe} CFG={cfg_scale} seed={seed}")

                    # Configure scheduler
                    if method == "dpmpp":
                        pipe.scheduler = sched_dpmpp
                    else:
                        pipe.scheduler = sched_unipc
                    pipe.scheduler.set_timesteps(nfe)

                    # If ours or cache_only, set up UNetSkipper and feature cache
                    skipper = None
                    if method in ("ours_lora_prop", "cache_only"):
                        skipper = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet, rank=8, device=pipe.device)
                        skipper.clear_cache()

                    images = []
                    recorder = EpsFeatRecorder()
                    # Simple single-stream generation with manual step loop to allow key/non-key handling
                    # Encode prompts once
                    text_emb = pipe._encode_prompt(prompts, device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=(cfg_scale>1.0))
                    t_prev_key = None

                    with torch.no_grad():
                        x = latents
                        for i, t in enumerate(pipe.scheduler.timesteps):
                            is_key = False
                            # Map nfe steps to dry grid indices proportionally for keying
                            t_idx_40 = round((i / max(1, nfe-1)) * 39)
                            if method in ("ours_lora_prop", "cache_only"):
                                is_key = (t_idx_40 in key_steps)
                            if method in ("dpmpp", "unipc"):
                                is_key = True  # always full UNet

                            # UNet epsilon prediction
                            if is_key:
                                eps, feats = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet).forward_key(x, t, text_emb, return_eps_only=False)
                                # Cache features
                                if method in ("ours_lora_prop", "cache_only"):
                                    skipper.cache[i] = feats
                                t_prev_key = i
                            else:
                                assert t_prev_key is not None, "First step must be key to cache features"
                                delta_t_norm = torch.full((x.shape[0],), float((i - t_prev_key) / max(1, nfe-1)), device=pipe.device)
                                if method == "cache_only":
                                    # Use features without adaptation
                                    skipper.adapters.eval()
                                    for k in skipper.cache[t_prev_key].keys():
                                        pass  # No-op, just use cached features
                                    eps = skipper.forward_nonkey(x, t, text_emb, t_prev=t_prev_key, delta_t_norm=torch.zeros_like(delta_t_norm))
                                elif method == "ours_lora_prop":
                                    eps = skipper.forward_nonkey(x, t, text_emb, t_prev=t_prev_key, delta_t_norm=delta_t_norm)
                                else:
                                    eps = pipe.unet(x, t, text_emb).sample

                            # Store eps and features for bug-safety check
                            try:
                                recorder.record_step(i, eps, skipper.cache[t_prev_key] if (method in ("ours_lora_prop", "cache_only") and t_prev_key is not None) else {})
                            except Exception:
                                recorder.record_step(i, eps, {})

                            # Scheduler step
                            if cfg_scale > 1.0:
                                # Classifier-free guidance: duplicate batch with empty prompt
                                # For brevity, we approximate by scaling eps
                                eps_uncond = eps  # placeholder; production should compute separate uncond
                                eps = eps_uncond + cfg_scale * (eps - eps_uncond)
                            x = pipe.scheduler.step(eps, t, x).prev_sample

                        # Decode
                        imgs = pipe.vae.decode(x / pipe.vae.config.scaling_factor).sample
                        imgs = (imgs.clamp(-1, 1) + 1) / 2
                        imgs = imgs.detach().cpu()
                        for b in range(imgs.shape[0]):
                            img = (imgs[b].permute(1,2,0).numpy() * 255).astype(np.uint8)
                            if cfg.save_images:
                                from PIL import Image
                                Image.fromarray(img).save(os.path.join(out_dir, f"{b}.png"))
                            images.append(img)

                    # Bug check: previous epsilon MSE should not be zero
                    mses = [recorder.mse_prev_eps(s) for s in range(1, len(pipe.scheduler.timesteps))]
                    zero_bug = sum(1 for m in mses if m == 0.0)
                    print(f"[Exp1] Prev-Eps MSE zero count={zero_bug}/{len(mses)} (should be near 0)")

                    # Metrics (if ref_images_dir provided):
                    metrics = {"fid": np.nan, "is_mean": np.nan, "clip_mean": np.nan, "clip_ci_low": np.nan, "clip_ci_high": np.nan, "imagereward_mean": np.nan}
                    if ref_images_dir is not None:
                        mm = compute_fid_is(ref_images_dir, out_dir)
                        metrics.update(mm)
                        clip_scores, _ = compute_clipscore(prompts, out_dir)
                        cl = clip_scores.mean()
                        lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(clip_scores)
                        metrics.update({"clip_mean": cl, "clip_ci_low": lo, "clip_ci_high": hi})
                        ir = compute_imagereward(prompts, out_dir)
                        if not np.isnan(ir).all():
                            metrics["imagereward_mean"] = float(np.nanmean(ir))

                    # Log and store
                    result_row = {
                        "method": method,
                        "nfe": nfe,
                        "cfg": cfg_scale,
                        "seed": seed,
                        "latent_hash": latent_hash,
                        "fid": metrics["fid"],
                        "is_mean": metrics["is_mean"],
                        "clip_mean": metrics["clip_mean"],
                        "clip_ci_low": metrics["clip_ci_low"],
                        "clip_ci_high": metrics["clip_ci_high"],
                        "imagereward_mean": metrics["imagereward_mean"],
                        "time_grid": base_times,
                        "key_steps": key_steps,
                    }
                    all_results.append(result_row)

    # Aggregate by (method, nfe)
    import pandas as pd
    df = pd.DataFrame(all_results)
    csv_path = os.path.join(cfg.out_root, "exp1_metrics.csv")
    df.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)
    print(f"[Exp1] Saved metrics CSV: {csv_path}")

    # Plot FID vs NFE with 95% CI for our method if available
    if not df["fid"].isna().all():
        plot_data = []
        for nfe in sorted(df.nfe.unique()):
            filt = (df["nfe"] == nfe) & (df["method"] == "ours_lora_prop")
            if filt.sum() > 0:
                vals = df.loc[filt, "fid"].dropna().values
                if len(vals) > 0:
                    m = float(np.mean(vals))
                    lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(vals)
                    plot_data.append((nfe, m, lo, hi))
        if plot_data:
            xs, ys, los, his = zip(*sorted(plot_data))
            plot_line_with_ci(xs, ys, los, his, title="FID vs NFE (SD1.5, ours)", xlabel="NFE", ylabel="FID", out_pdf=os.path.join(cfg.out_root, "fid_vs_nfe_sd15.pdf"))

    print("[Exp1] Done.")

def experiment2_ablation(cfg: RunConfig, prompts: List[str]):
