    dry_n = min(8, len(prompts))
    dry_latents = identical_latents(pipe, dry_n, seed=777)

    def dry_get_features(step_idx: int) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
        num_steps = 40
        from diffusers import DDIMScheduler
        ddim = DDIMScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config)
        ddim.set_timesteps(num_steps)
        t = ddim.timesteps[step_idx].to(pipe.device)
        feats: Dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {}
        hooks = []
        for i, db in enumerate(pipe.unet.down_blocks):
            hooks.append(db.register_forward_hook(lambda m, inp, out, i=i: feats.__setitem__(f"down_{i}", out.detach().cpu())))
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = pipe.unet(sample=dry_latents, timestep=t, encoder_hidden_states=pipe._encode_prompt(prompts[:dry_n], device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=False))
        for h in hooks:
            h.remove()
        return feats

    deltaF, layer_ids = compute_deltaF_heatmap(dry_get_features, n_steps=40)
    key_timewarp = greedy_timewarp_key_selection(deltaF, K=3, stratify_bins=4)
    key_uniform = [round(i) for i in np.linspace(1, 39, 3)]
    key_front = [1, 2, 3]
    plot_heatmap(deltaF, title="ΔF Heatmap (Ablation)", xlabel="Step", ylabel="Layer", out_pdf=os.path.join(cfg.out_root, "deltaF_heatmap_ablation.pdf"), key_steps=key_timewarp)

    # Compare cache-only vs LoRA-Prop, ranks and INT8
    ranks = [4, 8, 16]
    adapter_modes = ["fp16", "int8"]
    nfe_list = [4, 6]

    rows = []
    for rank in ranks:
        for nfe in nfe_list:
            for mode in adapter_modes:
                for schedule_name, key_steps in [("timewarp", key_timewarp), ("uniform", key_uniform), ("front", key_front)]:
                    for method in ["cache_only", "ours_lora_prop"]:
                        seed = 23
                        base_sched = sched_unipc
                        base_sched.set_timesteps(nfe)
                        latents = identical_latents(pipe, len(prompts), seed)
                        out_dir = os.path.join(cfg.out_root, f"exp2_{method}_{schedule_name}_r{rank}_{mode}_nfe{nfe}")
                        ensure_dir(out_dir)
                        skipper = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet, rank=rank, device=pipe.device)
                        if mode == "int8":
                            # Attempt INT8 with torch.quantization for adapters only (CPU) or bitsandbytes for GPU
                            try:
                                import bitsandbytes as bnb
                                for name, m in skipper.adapters.named_modules():
                                    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                                        # Replace with 8-bit Linear if possible; otherwise keep FP
                                        pass
                                print("[Exp2] bitsandbytes found; adapters can be INT8 on GPU if implemented.")
                            except Exception:
                                # Fallback: dynamic quantization on CPU if moved to CPU
                                print("[Exp2] bitsandbytes not found; using FP for adapters.")
                        skipper.clear_cache()

                        # Manual loop
                        text_emb = pipe._encode_prompt(prompts, device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=True)
                        with torch.no_grad():
                            x = latents
                            t_prev_key = None
                            eps_errs = []
                            for i, t in enumerate(pipe.scheduler.timesteps):
                                t_idx_40 = round((i / max(1, nfe-1)) * 39)
                                is_key = t_idx_40 in key_steps
                                if is_key:
                                    eps, feats = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet).forward_key(x, t, text_emb, return_eps_only=False)
                                    skipper.cache[i] = feats
                                    t_prev_key = i
                                else:
                                    delta_t_norm = torch.full((x.shape[0],), float((i - t_prev_key) / max(1, nfe-1)), device=pipe.device)
                                    if method == "cache_only":
                                        eps = skipper.forward_nonkey(x, t, text_emb, t_prev=t_prev_key, delta_t_norm=torch.zeros_like(delta_t_norm))
                                    else:
                                        eps = skipper.forward_nonkey(x, t, text_emb, t_prev=t_prev_key, delta_t_norm=delta_t_norm)
                                # Compare eps vs full unet eps (teacher) for error curves
                                eps_full = pipe.unet(x, t, text_emb).sample
                                eps_errs.append(float(F.mse_loss(eps.float(), eps_full.float()).item()))
                                x = pipe.scheduler.step(eps, t, x).prev_sample

                        # Decode only a few images for metrics efficiency
                        imgs = pipe.vae.decode(x / pipe.vae.config.scaling_factor).sample
                        imgs = (imgs.clamp(-1, 1) + 1) / 2
                        imgs = imgs.detach().cpu()
                        for b in range(min(4, imgs.shape[0])):

                        xs = list(range(len(eps_errs)))
                        plot_line_with_ci(xs, eps_errs, eps_errs, eps_errs, title=f"Epsilon MSE per step ({method}, {schedule_name}, r{rank}, {mode}, NFE={nfe})", xlabel="Step", ylabel="MSE", out_pdf=os.path.join(cfg.out_root, f"epsilon_mse_{method}_{schedule_name}_r{rank}_{mode}_nfe{nfe}.pdf"))
                        rows.append({"method": method, "schedule": schedule_name, "rank": rank, "mode": mode, "nfe": nfe, "eps_mse_mean": float(np.mean(eps_errs))})

    import pandas as pd
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

    print("[Exp2] Done.")

def count_flops_unet(pipe) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    try:
        from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis
        sample = torch.randn(1, pipe.unet.config.in_channels, pipe.unet.config.sample_size, pipe.unet.config.sample_size, device=pipe.device, dtype=pipe.unet.dtype)
        t = torch.tensor([1.0], device=pipe.device, dtype=torch.float32)  # dummy
        txt = pipe._encode_prompt(["test"], device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=False)
        flops_full = FlopCountAnalysis(pipe.unet, (sample, t, txt)).total()
        # Non-key: use only mid+up path via skipper
        skipper = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet, rank=8, device=pipe.device)
        # For FlopCountAnalysis, wrap forward_nonkey
        class NonKeyWrapper(nn.Module):
            def __init__(self, sk):
                super().__init__()
                self.sk = sk
            def forward(self, sample, t, txt):
                # Need a cached feature shape; emulate with running a key forward once
                eps, feats = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet).forward_key(sample, t, txt, return_eps_only=False)
                self.sk.cache[0] = feats
                dt = torch.tensor([0.5], device=sample.device)
                return self.sk.forward_nonkey(sample, t, txt, t_prev=0, delta_t_norm=dt)
        wrapper = NonKeyWrapper(skipper)
        flops_nonkey = FlopCountAnalysis(wrapper, (sample, t, txt)).total()
        return int(flops_full), int(flops_nonkey)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[Exp3] FlopCountAnalysis unavailable or failed: {e}")
        return -1, -1


def measure_throughput(pipe, method: str = "ours_lora_prop", nfe: int = 4, cfg_scale: float = 7.0, iters: int = 30) -> Dict[str, float]:
    pipe.set_progress_bar_config(disable=True)
    latents = identical_latents(pipe, 1, seed=1234)
    text_emb = pipe._encode_prompt(["A photo of a cat"], device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=True)
    skipper = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet, rank=8, device=pipe.device) if method in ("ours_lora_prop", "cache_only") else None
    # Warm up
    for _ in range(5):
        with torch.no_grad():
            x = latents
            pipe.scheduler.set_timesteps(nfe)
            for i, t in enumerate(pipe.scheduler.timesteps):
                eps = pipe.unet(x, t, text_emb).sample
                x = pipe.scheduler.step(eps, t, x).prev_sample
    torch.cuda.synchronize() if pipe.device.type == 'cuda' else None

    # Measure
    times = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        t0 = time.time()
        with torch.no_grad():
            x = latents
            pipe.scheduler.set_timesteps(nfe)
            for i, t in enumerate(pipe.scheduler.timesteps):
                eps = pipe.unet(x, t, text_emb).sample
                x = pipe.scheduler.step(eps, t, x).prev_sample
        torch.cuda.synchronize() if pipe.device.type == 'cuda' else None
        times.append(time.time() - t0)
    it_s = 1.0 / (np.mean(times) + 1e-9)
    return {"images_per_sec": float(it_s), "mean_sec": float(np.mean(times)), "std_sec": float(np.std(times))}


def export_onnx_models(pipe, out_dir: str):
    ensure_dir(out_dir)
    sample = torch.randn(1, pipe.unet.config.in_channels, pipe.unet.config.sample_size, pipe.unet.config.sample_size, device=pipe.device, dtype=pipe.unet.dtype)
    t = torch.tensor([1.0], device=pipe.device, dtype=torch.float32)
    txt = pipe._encode_prompt(["test"], device=pipe.device, num_images_per_prompt=1, do_classifier_free_guidance=False)

    # Ensure no Python assert inside traced graph
    # If needed, pre-check shapes here (outside graph)
    assert sample.dim() == 4 and t.dim() == 1 and txt.dim() == 3

    key_path = os.path.join(out_dir, "unet_key.onnx")
    torch.onnx.export(
        pipe.unet, (sample, t, txt), key_path,
        input_names=["sample", "timestep", "encoder_hidden_states"],
        output_names=["eps_out"],
        opset_version=17,
        dynamic_axes={"sample": {0: "b"}, "timestep": {0: "b"}, "encoder_hidden_states": {0: "b"}},
        do_constant_folding=True,
    )
    print(f"[Exp3] Exported key-step UNet to {key_path}")

    # Export non-key wrapper
    skipper = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet, rank=8, device=pipe.device)
    eps, feats = UNetSkipper(pipe.unet).forward_key(sample, t, txt, return_eps_only=False)
    skipper.cache[0] = feats

    class NonKeyWrapper(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, sk):
            super().__init__()
            self.sk = sk
        def forward(self, sample, t, txt, delta_t_norm):
            return self.sk.forward_nonkey(sample, t, txt, t_prev=0, delta_t_norm=delta_t_norm)

    wrapper = NonKeyWrapper(skipper).to(pipe.device)
    dt = torch.tensor([0.5], device=pipe.device)
    nonkey_path = os.path.join(out_dir, "unet_nonkey.onnx")
    torch.onnx.export(
        wrapper, (sample, t, txt, dt), nonkey_path,
        input_names=["sample", "timestep", "encoder_hidden_states", "delta_t_norm"],
        output_names=["eps_out"],
        opset_version=17,
        dynamic_axes={"sample": {0: "b"}, "timestep": {0: "b"}, "encoder_hidden_states": {0: "b"}, "delta_t_norm": {0: "b"}},
        do_constant_folding=True,
    )
    print(f"[Exp3] Exported non-key UNet to {nonkey_path}")

class TinyUNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ch=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(4, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.mid = nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.conv_out = nn.Conv2d(ch, 4, 1)
    def forward(self, x, t_emb):
        h = F.silu(self.conv1(x))
        h = F.silu(self.conv2(h))
        h = F.silu(self.mid(h + t_emb.view(-1,1,1,1)))
        return self.conv_out(h)

experimental_analysis.analysis_report:
Analysis report for LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp)

Executive summary
- Goal: Validate whether LoRA-Prop (+ Time-Warp) can preserve quality at extreme low-step regimes (3–8 NFEs) while reducing per-step FLOPs, without retraining the base model.
- What actually ran: A toy sanity run using the provided experimental code (Tiny/“toy” setup), including Time-Warp key-step discovery, brief adapter training, and an evaluation that compared cache-only vs LoRA-Prop on a lightweight surrogate. Full-scale SD1.5/DiT evaluations with COCO/ImageNet and FID/IS/CLIPScore were not executed in the captured logs.
- Headline outcome on the toy run: LoRA-Prop did not show a quality advantage over cache-only (identical average MSE). Throughput showed the expected ordering (cache-only fastest, LoRA-Prop faster than full UNet), but LoRA-Prop was much slower than cache-only. Therefore, the current run does not demonstrate a clear advantage of the proposed method; results are inconclusive pending full-scale experiments.

Experimental setup actually executed
- Implementation: The code base matches the described verification plan: it implements Time-Warp key-step discovery via ΔF heatmaps, LoRA-Prop adapters with time embedding, a UNetSkipper for non-key steps, and evaluation utilities (bootstrapping, paired tests, GFLOPs counting, ONNX export hooks). A bug-fix path for zero-MSE artifacts in feature/epsilon comparisons is included and exercised in a separate quick functional test.
- Run contents (from logs):
  - Time-Warp (toy) key-step discovery produced varying key-step selections across sub-runs (e.g., [5, 7, 9] initially; [1, 4, 9] in evaluation), consistent with different dry passes and seeds.
  - Adapter training (toy) for 3 epochs with a final loss ≈ 0.001107 (constant across epochs), suggesting little to no learning in the toy setting.
  - Evaluation (toy):
    • Avg MSE (cache-only): 0.006393
    • Avg MSE (LoRA-Prop): 0.006393 (no improvement vs cache-only)
    • Throughput (images/sec): full=22.09; cache-only=455.61; LoRA-Prop=64.79
    • Derived speedups: LoRA-Prop ≈ 2.93× faster than full UNet; cache-only ≈ 20.6× faster than full UNet; LoRA-Prop ≈ 7× slower than cache-only.
- Artifacts: ΔF heatmap, MSE bar plot, throughput bar plot, and a toy adapter training curve were saved. The quick functional test also verified the zero-MSE bug fix (no zero MSEs observed across steps in that test).

Comparison to planned verification policy
- Planned Experiment 1 (quality/statistical validation on SD1.5/DiT with COCO/ImageNet) was not present in the captured run; thus, no FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward, no multi-seed bootstrapped CIs, and no hypothesis tests vs strong baselines at matched NFEs were reported.
- Planned Experiment 2 (mechanisms/ablations) partially overlapped in spirit: ΔF heatmaps and key-step selection were exercised in toy form. However, key ablations (ranks r∈{4,8,16}, INT8 vs FP16, Time-Warp vs uniform/front-loaded schedules with end-to-end quality) and epsilon/feature error diagnostics against full UNet on SD1.5/DiT were not reported.
- Planned Experiment 3 (systems validation with GFLOPs accounting, A100 throughput, mobile latency and ONNX/CoreML parity) was not executed in the captured logs. Only toy throughput was observed.

Interpretation of toy outcomes
- Quality proxy (MSE) shows LoRA-Prop equals cache-only on this toy task. This suggests the adapters did not learn a beneficial extrapolation relative to simply reusing cached features. Potential reasons:
  1) Toy setting is too simple; identity/caching may already be near-optimal, leaving little headroom for extrapolation to help.
  2) The very short/limited training (3 epochs) and tiny data may be insufficient for the adapters to learn useful time-conditioned projections.
  3) Zero-initialized residual adapters preserve the base behavior; without a strong learning signal or sufficient capacity, the optimizer may converge to near-identity.
  4) Mismatch between the toy loss and the behavior of a real diffusion UNet with skip/mid-block dynamics.
- Throughput behavior aligns with expectations from the design:
  - Cache-only is a pure reuse shortcut and, on the toy, avoids almost all computation, hence the large speedup.
  - LoRA-Prop adds lightweight compute (rank-r adapters and a partial forward) to improve quality at non-key steps; it is faster than full UNet but slower than cache-only.
  - On real models at 3–8 steps, LoRA-Prop is intended to recover quality where cache-only blurs/fails; the toy run does not reproduce this failure mode, and thus does not showcase LoRA-Prop’s intended advantage.

Limitations and deviations
- No real-model results (SD1.5/DiT/ADM) on COCO/ImageNet were reported; therefore, core claims around FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward, robustness vs guidance, and generalization to DreamBooth checkpoints remain unverified here.
- No GFLOPs accounting or mobile latency were measured in this run. The expected results from the method description (e.g., FID within +0.3 of 20-step DDIM at NFE=4; 1.8–2.3× throughput vs FasterDiffusion; >4× vs vanilla DPM-Solver++-4; <1100 ms on iPhone 14 Pro) cannot be confirmed or contradicted by the toy results.
- Minor reproducibility note: key-step sets differed between the initial and evaluation dry passes (e.g., [5,7,9] vs [1,4,9]). This is expected if different seeds/batches are used, but for strict reproducibility at scale, fixing the dry batch/seed and logging hashes is recommended.

Does the new method demonstrate a clear advantage?
- Based on the captured toy run: No. LoRA-Prop did not improve the quality proxy (MSE) over cache-only and was much slower than cache-only, although it was faster than the full model. This result is not representative of the intended operating regime; the toy setup likely failed to expose the quality degradation that LoRA-Prop is designed to mitigate at low NFEs.
- Conclusion: The present evidence is inconclusive. A clear advantage must be established on real models/datasets as per the verification policy.

Recommendations to complete the verification
- Execute Experiment 1 on SD1.5 (COCO val5k) and DiT-XL/2 (ImageNet val50k) with:
  - NFE ∈ {3,4,6,8}, guidance ∈ {3,5,7,12}, identical latents/time-grids.
  - Baselines: DPM-Solver++/UniPC at matched NFEs, AdaptiveDiffusion, FasterDiffusion, distilled-8.
  - Metrics: FID/IS, CLIPScore, ImageReward with 95% bootstrap CIs and paired tests (Holm–Bonferroni corrections).
  - Acceptance criteria: at NFE=4, FID within +0.3 of 20-step DDIM and ≥1.0 better than best non-LoRA baseline with p<0.01; no CLIPScore/ImageReward degradation.
- Execute Experiment 2 ablations:
  - Time-Warp vs uniform/front-loaded keys at fixed K; report epsilon/feature errors and final FID deltas.
  - Ranks r∈{4,8,16}; INT8 vs FP16 adapters; verify ΔFID ≤ 0.3 for INT8.
  - Publish ΔF heatmaps and key indices; confirm monotonic quality with NFE.
- Execute Experiment 3 systems validation:
  - GFLOPs accounting (fvcore) for key vs non-key calls; measured throughput on A100; peak memory.
  - ONNX/CoreML parity checks; mobile latency on iPhone 14 Pro with median/p95 under target budgets.
- Add a generalization check: plug the same adapters into 5 DreamBooth SD1.5 checkpoints and verify ΔFID ≤ 0.5 with no CLIPScore drop at NFE {4,6}.

Bottom line
- The method conceptually targets a real gap (extreme low-step operation with reduced per-step FLOPs). The implementation and verification scaffolding are in place. However, the only recorded run is toy-level and does not demonstrate the hypothesized advantages. To claim a clear advantage, run the full verification suite; success criteria are already defined in the plan and can decisively confirm or reject the method’s benefits.

consistency_feedback:
Summary: The methodology is clearly articulated and the planned experiments are well motivated, but the presented experimental results do not substantiate the main claims. Most reported numbers come from a synthetic, toy setup with PSNR rather than the stated core metrics (FID/IS/CLIPScore) on real diffusion models. Several implementation issues and missing statistical analyses undermine confidence that the proposed approach maintains quality at extreme low-step regimes or yields the claimed speedups in real settings.

Key inconsistencies and gaps
- Metrics mismatch with claims: The headline claims (e.g., “FID within +0.3 of DDIM-20 at 4 steps; ≈1.0 better than DPM-Solver++-4”) are not supported by the presented results. Only toy PSNR/MSE on synthetic patterns are reported; no FID/IS/CLIPScore, no ImageReward, and no comparisons on SD1.5/DiT/ADM are shown.
- Statistical rigor missing: The design promises multi-seed runs, bootstrap CIs, and paired t-tests. The logs show single-seed or single-run numbers without CIs, p-values, or effect sizes. Throughput and latency lack confidence intervals and variance estimates.
- Baselines incomplete: In the toy results, only "full", "cache", and "loraprop" are compared. No DPM-Solver++/UniPC baselines at equal NFEs, no AdaptiveDiffusion, and no distillation student are reported as in the plan. Thus, competitive positioning is unsubstantiated.
- Identical quality across methods: PSNR/MSE are virtually identical across full, cache, and LoRA-Prop for all NFEs and guidance scales. This suggests either the metric is insensitive in the toy setup, the adapter’s contribution is being bypassed, or a bug causes the non-key path to behave equivalently to caching.
- Paradoxical step-quality trend: PSNR slightly decreases as NFE increases (e.g., 5.633 at NFE=4 vs 5.613 at NFE=8). While a toy scheduler can exhibit such behavior, it warrants investigation and undermines claims about solver quality preservation at low steps.
- Key-step discovery anomaly: Selected key indices are [1,2,3] (very early steps only), contradicting the stated goal of covering early noise and late details. This questions the effectiveness of ΔF-based selection (in this toy instantiation) and suggests the selection criterion needs validation.
- Methodological bug in light path: In the toy model’s light forward, a new Conv2d is instantiated inside forward on every call. This is a major methodological flaw that breaks determinism and training logic. The head should use a fixed, registered module constructed in __init__, not created anew each forward.
- INT8 reporting incomplete: The microbench function is designed to report INT8 speedup and feature-error correlations, but the logs do not include the actual INT8 speedup value or the correlation numbers (e.g., Pearson r between feature MSE and epsilon/pixel error). Saved plots are referenced without numeric summaries.
- ONNX export failure: The light-path export error (input channel mismatch) highlights integration inconsistencies between heavy and light paths, suggesting the deployment claims need further engineering validation before they can be substantiated.

Statistical analysis concerns
- No reported p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes for any quality metric. 
- No bootstrap CIs for FID (not computed), despite being promised. 
- Throughput/latency lack variability estimates and controlled warmup/cooldown reporting beyond a brief description.

Experimental design issues and confounders
- Toy setup may not be sensitive enough: PSNR on synthetic patterns may not reflect the quality degradations the method is meant to avoid (texture blur at high guidance, prompt-length sensitivity). This likely explains the indistinguishable PSNR across methods.
- Guidance-scale evaluation not meaningful: In the toy model, classifier-free guidance may not influence outputs meaningfully, explaining the flat curves. This cannot be used to support robustness to guidance in real diffusion systems.
- Feature-propagation head likely dominates: Because the light path’s head is not properly trained or fixed, it may ignore the supplied summaries, making cache vs LoRA-Prop indistinguishable in practice. This confounds interpretation of quality results.

Actionable recommendations
1) Run the planned real-model evaluations:
   - SD 1.5 on COCO-val (5k prompts) with FID/IS/CLIPScore, ImageReward; report mean±95% CI and paired tests vs baselines at NFEs {3,4,6,8}. 
   - Include DPM-Solver++ and UniPC, FasterDiffusion (encoder propagation), AdaptiveDiffusion step skipping, and an 8-step distilled student.
2) Fix the light-path implementation:
   - Move the 1x1 conv (and any light-path layers) into the model’s __init__ so they are fixed modules, not instantiated in forward.
   - Verify that the epsilon head meaningfully uses the summarized features (e.g., ablate summaries to zeros to confirm a measurable drop; measure effect sizes).
3) Validate key-step discovery:
   - Inspect and plot ΔF over time to ensure both early and late information-rich steps are selected. Compare greedy ΔF vs uniform and front-loaded schedules at equal NFEs.
4) Report proper statistical support:
   - For quality metrics, report µ±σ across ≥3 seeds, 95% CIs (bootstrap for FID), and paired t-tests vs best non-LoRA baseline with pre-registered significance (e.g., p<0.01). Report effect sizes.
   - For throughput/latency, report medians with IQR or mean±95% CI over many runs; control for warm-up.
5) Microbench rigor:
   - Provide per-step FLOPs measured with torch.profiler or fvcore and validate against analytic counts. 
   - Report INT8 speedup and the delta in quality (e.g., ΔFID, ΔCLIPScore) with CIs.
   - Quantify correlations: layer-wise feature MSE vs epsilon error and pixel-space metrics (LPIPS/PSNR), and provide Pearson r with CIs.
6) Ablations and sensitivity:
   - r in {4,8,16}, K in {2,3,4}, INT8 vs FP16, and different time-grid strategies with full metrics and statistical tests. 
   - Sweep guidance scales and prompt lengths on the real model; examine where LoRA-Prop diverges from encoder caching.
7) Fairness and controls:
   - Match NFEs and guidance scales across all methods; fix seeds; record exact time-grids used. Ensure identical conditioning and VAE configs.
8) Deployment validation:
   - Resolve ONNX export issues (channel mismatches); provide end-to-end mobile or proxy latency with the light path active, and quantify accuracy impact under quantization. 
9) Sanity checks:
   - Verify that LoRA-Prop actually changes outputs versus caching in a controlled setting (e.g., measure non-key step epsilon and feature differences). 
   - Ensure increasing NFEs improves or at least does not systematically degrade quality in the real pipeline.

Bottom line: The current toy results are internally consistent in the sense that compute decreases for cache/LoRA-Prop and quality appears unchanged, but this very lack of differentiation indicates the evaluation is not probing the claimed advantages. Without real-model (SD/DiT/ADM) metrics, statistical tests, and corrected implementation of the light path, the key scientific claims remain unsupported.

Summary: The current experimental results are insufficient and partially inconsistent with the stated claims. Most core claims (FID/IS/CLIPScore parity at 3–8 steps, throughput/GFLOPs reductions, robustness, statistical significance) are not empirically demonstrated on real diffusion models/datasets; reported numbers are synthetic sanity checks. One reported metric (Prev-Eps MSE = 0.0) indicates a likely evaluation bug. The ONNX parity check and ΔF key-step selection were executed, but do not substantiate the main quality/speed claims.

- Statistical support missing: No FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward results on COCO-val5k or ImageNet-val; no confidence intervals, no paired tests, no effect sizes. H1/H2 cannot be evaluated.

- Remove Python assert from traced forward; use torch._assert or pre-export shape checks.

5) Generalization checks
- Test adapters on DreamBooth-finetuned checkpoints without retraining; report ΔFID and text alignment metrics with CIs; include failure cases.

If these improvements are executed and the specified hypotheses are statistically supported across datasets and seeds, the methodology could robustly substantiate the paper’s claims. As currently presented, the evidence is preliminary and not adequate to support the main conclusions.

Overall assessment: The current experimental results do not consistently support the stated scientific claims. While the methodological plan is thorough and well-specified, the actually presented results are toy-scale, internally contradictory in places, and lack the statistical evidence and real-model evaluations required to substantiate the performance and quality claims.

Key inconsistencies and gaps
- Claims vs evidence mismatch:
  - The core claims (near-teacher FID at 4 steps, 1.8–2.3× throughput over encoder-propagation, >4× over DPM-Solver++-4, <1100 ms on iPhone) are not supported by measured results. The only reported numbers are from a toy run, with no FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward, no bootstrap CIs, and no hypothesis tests.
  - The toy evaluation reports identical average MSE for cache-only and LoRA-Prop (0.006393 each), contradicting the acceptance criterion that LoRA-Prop should significantly outperform cache-only on feature/epsilon errors and final metrics.
  - Throughput in the toy run shows cache-only >> ours >> full, contrary to expected speedups over strong baselines; moreover, no comparisons to DPM-Solver++/UniPC/FasterDiffusion or distillation are provided.

- Internal contradictions/implementation red flags:
  - Key-step selection is inconsistent within the same run log: initially [5,7,9], later reported [1,4,9]. This suggests nondeterminism or logging/selection mismatch.
  - Training loss remains constant across epochs (0.001107 for 3 epochs) and the final cache-only vs ours MSE are identical, suggesting adapters may not be in the computation graph, not updated, or not used during non-key steps.
  - The provided sampling loop contains a critical CFG bug: eps_uncond = eps (placeholder), making guidance effectively a no-op and invalidating any CFG-sensitive quality claims.
  - No verification that the non-key path actually skips down-blocks and uses adapters; without per-step FLOPs/profiler traces, it’s unclear whether the intended compute savings occur in practice.

- Statistical and reporting issues:
  - No bootstrap confidence intervals, no paired tests (t-test or Wilcoxon), no effect sizes, and no multiple-comparison corrections on any real metrics. Monotonicity with NFE is not tested.
  - No seed-stratified, paired experimental runs on real datasets/models. No logging of latent hashes, time-grid hashes, or key-step indices in the results section.

- Data/benchmarking concerns:
  - Only toy experiments are reported; no evaluations on SD1.5, DiT-XL/2, or ADM-256 as specified.
  - No FID against COCO or ImageNet references; no CLIPScore/ImageReward; no ImageNet IS.
  - No GFLOPs accounting (analytic vs measured), memory, or mobile latency data.

Actionable recommendations
1) Validate correctness of the LoRA-Prop path
- Add unit tests to ensure adapters are trained and used:
  - Freeze base UNet, train adapters; verify adapter parameters change (non-zero grad norms) and loss decreases across iterations.
  - Compare epsilon MSE for cache-only vs ours at non-key steps using the full UNet as teacher; expect ours < cache-only. If equal, instrument the forward_nonkey to assert adapters are invoked and delta_t flows through.
  - Introduce a rank-0 or zeroed-adapter ablation; if results match “ours,” the adapter path is being bypassed.
- Fix CFG implementation: compute unconditional branch by actually encoding empty prompts and forming eps = eps_uncond + s*(eps_cond − eps_uncond). The current placeholder invalidates guidance-related robustness claims.

2) Re-run Experiment 1 with real models/datasets and rigorous statistics
- SD1.5 on COCO-val5k and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-val50k with identical latents/time-grids across methods, NFE ∈ {3,4,6,8}, CFG ∈ {3,5,7,12}, ≥3 seeds.
- Report FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward with 95% bootstrap CIs; perform paired t-tests vs best non-LoRA baseline per (NFE, CFG), Holm–Bonferroni corrected; include Cohen’s d.
- Verify monotonicity (FID vs NFE) with Kendall’s tau and CI overlap checks.

3) Mechanism and ablations (Experiment 2)
- Time-Warp vs uniform/front-loaded: show significant FID gains at fixed NFE (p<0.01). Release ΔF heatmaps and selected key-step indices; ensure deterministic selection by fixing seeds and using a disjoint dry batch.
- Ranks r ∈ {4,8,16}, INT8 vs FP16 adapters: quantify ΔFID, ΔCLIPScore with CIs; acceptance ΔFID ≤ 0.3 and no significant CLIPScore drop.

5) Data hygiene and reproducibility
- Release exact file lists with SHA256 for COCO/ImageNet, latent seeds/hashes, time-grid hashes, key-step indices, and environment hashes.
- Ensure the key-step selection is deterministic and consistent across logs; remove conflicting prints.

6) Additional controls
- Include a “full-UNet at all steps” control on the warped time-grid to isolate the impact of warping vs feature propagation.
- Add a “reuse-only” baseline (strict encoder caching) under the same key-steps to quantify extrapolation benefit.
- Report DreamBooth generalization deltas with CIs as claimed.

Conclusion: The current toy results are insufficient and contain inconsistencies that undermine the conclusions. Implement the fixes above, then execute the three planned experiments with full statistical rigor and systems measurements to substantiate the method’s claims.

Overall assessment: The current “Experimental Results” do not provide real, statistically supported evidence for the main claims. Most reported numbers are either “Expected” (projected) or come from a toy run that contradicts the hypothesis (no quality gain over cache-only). As such, the results are not yet internally consistent nor sufficient to support the scientific claims.

Key inconsistencies and gaps
- No real quality metrics reported: FID/IS/CLIPScore/ImageReward for SD1.5/DiT/ImageNet/COCO are not provided. The document lists acceptance criteria and procedures but does not present measured outcomes with confidence intervals or p-values.
- Toy-only evaluation contradicts the claim: The toy run reports identical MSE for cache-only vs LoRA-Prop (0.006393 vs 0.006393), implying no benefit from the adapters, which is inconsistent with the proposed mechanism and expected improvements.
- Inconsistent key-step selection: Logs show different key sets within the same session ([5,7,9] vs [1,4,9]). This suggests non-determinism or inconsistent mapping between the warped grid and the solver steps. It undermines reproducibility and makes paired comparisons invalid.
- Classifier-free guidance implemented incorrectly in code comments (“eps_uncond = eps” placeholder). Using the same epsilon for cond/uncond will distort image quality and invalidate any CLIPScore/FID comparisons.
- No statistical analysis despite plans: No bootstrap CIs, no paired t-tests/Wilcoxon, no Holm–Bonferroni correction, no effect sizes, and no monotonic trend tests are actually reported.
- Systems claims are unsubstantiated: No GFLOPs accounting or profiler validation on real UNets; throughput and latency are only from a toy setup. No mobile/CoreML parity or on-device latency measurements are shown.
- Possible training/measurement bugs: Adapter training loss is constant across epochs, and the adapter shows no benefit over cache-only in the toy evaluation. This hints at zero/vanishing gradients, miswired loss, or incorrect feature taps. Also, the previously noted zero-MSE artifact is not convincingly ruled out in real settings.

Statistical analysis concerns
- Missing CIs and hypothesis tests: For each dataset/NFE/CFG, you need 95% bootstrap CIs and paired tests vs best baseline, corrected for multiple CFGs. None are presented.
- Effect sizes absent: Report Cohen’s d alongside p-values. This is not shown.
- Monotonicity claims not tested: No Kendall’s tau test or CI overlap checks are presented.

Experimental design issues
- Baselines and controls not executed: DPM-Solver++, UniPC, AdaptiveDiffusion, FasterDiffusion, and distilled-8 should be run at matched NFEs/CFG with identical latents/time-grids. Only toy results are shown.
- Time-grid control unclear: The mapping from NFE timesteps to the DDIM-40 dry grid for key selection must be deterministic and fixed per model. The current rounding-based mapping may skip the first step and changes across runs, leading to cache misses and biased comparisons.
- CFG implementation error: Correct CFG needs separate unconditional and conditional forward passes per step; the placeholder collapses to a single stream and invalidates quality metrics.
- First-step key requirement: Non-key steps need a preceding cached key step. Ensure step 0 is always selected as key to avoid undefined behavior at the start.
- Feature tapping correctness: In diffusers UNets, down_blocks often return tuples of residuals. Forward hooks on whole modules may capture incompatible shapes or non-final tensors. Mis-specified taps can corrupt ΔF, training targets, and MSE.

Data/measurement quality concerns
- No evidence that FID reference sets were correctly loaded (counts/sha256). No per-run CSVs or hashes are shown.
- The adapter training shows flat loss; verify gradient flow, parameter updates, and target construction. Confirm non-key target features F_l(t) and inputs F_l(t′) are aligned to the same spatial resolution and normalization.
- Epsilon/feature error comparisons against a full UNet teacher are not reported (beyond toy). Without these, mechanism validation is incomplete.

Systems validation gaps
- GFLOPs: No analytic vs measured FLOPs reported for full vs non-key paths. The toy code doesn’t reflect SD1.5/DiT compute structure.
- Throughput: Only toy throughput is reported; does not translate to real models. No variance across runs, batch sizes, or CFG.
- INT8: No measured quality deltas (ΔFID, ΔCLIPScore) or speedups for adapters-only INT8 on real models.
- Mobile: No ONNX/CoreML parity checks (PSNR/MAE/LPIPS) and no on-device latency results.

Actionable recommendations
1) Fix core correctness issues before re-running:
  - Implement proper CFG with unconditional and conditional branches per step. Validate with small prompt sets by checking that images change sensibly with guidance scale.
  - Enforce deterministic key-step mapping: fix the dry ΔF grid once per model, seed all RNGs, include step 0 as a key, and document the index mapping from NFE to dry grid. Persist key indices to JSON and reuse.
  - Verify feature taps: Hook specific tensors that are used as skip connections (e.g., outputs of ResBlocks whose activations feed up_blocks). Log tensor shapes and norms; ensure matching shapes between cached F_l(t′) and target F_l(t).
  - Validate teacher comparisons: For non-key steps, compute eps_full from the full UNet and log per-step epsilon MSE; ensure it is non-zero and decreases with the adapter vs cache-only.
  - Check training: Ensure only adapter weights are trainable, loss uses correct targets, and gradients are non-zero. Add unit tests that show the adapter changes outputs (e.g., finite-difference sanity check) and that training reduces held-out feature-MSE by >20%.

2) Minimal real-data sanity run (prior to full-scale):
  - SD1.5 on 500 COCO-val prompts, seeds={11,23,47}, NFE={4,6}, CFG={5,7}. Compare ours vs DPM-Solver++ and FasterDiffusion at matched time-grids/latents.
  - Report: FID (with correct COCO reference), CLIPScore means and 95% bootstrap CIs; paired t-test and Wilcoxon vs best baseline with Holm–Bonferroni across CFGs; Cohen’s d.
  - Mechanism: Plot epsilon-MSE and feature-MSE per step; show that LoRA-Prop < cache-only with p<0.01.
  - Trend: Check monotonic decrease of FID with NFE via Kendall’s tau.

3) Full Experiment 1 as specified once sanity checks pass:
  - COCO-5k and ImageNet-50k with all baselines, identical latents/time-grids, and three seeds. Provide full tables with CIs, p-values, and effect sizes. Explicitly test acceptance criteria (e.g., +0.3 FID vs DDIM-20 at NFE=4, ≥1.0 better than best baseline, p<0.01).

4) Ablations and robustness (Experiment 2):
  - Time-Warp vs uniform/front-loaded at fixed K: show statistically significant FID gains (p<0.01) and visible alignment to ΔF peaks.
  - Rank r and INT8: quantify ΔFID and ΔCLIPScore with CIs; require ΔFID ≤ 0.3 for INT8.
  - Publish ΔF heatmaps and key-step indices to support reproducibility.

5) Systems validation (Experiment 3):
  - Provide analytic GFLOPs per step and total per image; cross-verify with torch.profiler (agreement within 5%). Report peak memory.
  - Throughput on A100 (batch=1,4) with 30-run mean±std for ours vs baselines and show the targeted 1.8–2.3× speedup over FasterDiffusion and >4× over vanilla DPM-Solver++ at NFE=4.
  - INT8 adapters: report speedups and ΔFID/CLIP CIs.
  - ONNX/CoreML parity and iPhone measurements: PSNR/MAE/LPIPS thresholds met on non-key outputs and final images; report median and p95 latency; target <1100 ms at 512×512, NFE=4.

6) Reproducibility hygiene:
  - Release file lists with SHA256, time-grids and key-step JSONs, per-run CSV/sqlite logs, environment hashes, and profiler traces. Include unit tests for the previous zero-MSE artifact and for ONNX parity.

Conclusion: As presented, the evidence is insufficient and internally inconsistent (toy results show no advantage; key-step selection varies; no real metrics/statistics). Implement the fixes above and rerun the planned experiments to provide statistically grounded, reproducible support for the claims.

@article{chen-2023-data,
 abstract = {Dataset distillation aims to minimize the time and memory needed for training
deep networks on large datasets, by creating a small set of synthetic images
that has a similar generalization performance to that of the full dataset.
However, current dataset distillation techniques fall short, showing a notable
performance gap when compared to training on the original data. In this work,
we are the first to argue that using just one synthetic subset for distillation
will not yield optimal generalization performance. This is because the training
dynamics of deep networks drastically change during the training. Hence,
multiple synthetic subsets are required to capture the training dynamics at
different phases of training. To address this issue, we propose Progressive
Dataset Distillation (PDD). PDD synthesizes multiple small sets of synthetic
images, each conditioned on the previous sets, and trains the model on the
cumulative union of these subsets without requiring additional training time.
Our extensive experiments show that PDD can effectively improve the performance
of existing dataset distillation methods by up to 4.3%. In addition, our method
for the first time enable generating considerably larger synthetic datasets.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.06982v1.pdf},
 author = {Xuxi Chen and Yu Yang and Zhangyang Wang and Baharan Mirzasoleiman},
 title = {Data Distillation Can Be Like Vodka: Distilling More Times For Better Quality},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{chen-2023-fast,
 abstract = {Discrete diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for high-quality
data generation. Despite their success in discrete spaces, such as text
generation tasks, the acceleration of discrete diffusion models remains
under-explored. In this paper, we propose discrete non-Markov diffusion models
(DNDM), which naturally induce the predetermined transition time set. This
enables a training-free sampling algorithm that significantly reduces the
number of function evaluations (i.e., calls to the neural network), making the
sampling process much faster. Furthermore, we study the transition from finite
to infinite step sampling, offering new insights into bridging the gap between
discrete and continuous-time processes for discrete diffusion models. Extensive
experiments on natural language generation and machine translation tasks
demonstrate the superior performance of our method in terms of both generation
speed and sample quality compared to existing methods for discrete diffusion
models.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.09193v3.pdf},
 author = {Zixiang Chen and Huizhuo Yuan and Yongqian Li and Yiwen Kou and Junkai Zhang and Quanquan Gu},
 title = {Fast Sampling via Discrete Non-Markov Diffusion Models with Predetermined Transition Time},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{hsiao-2024-plug,
 abstract = {Diffusion models have shown tremendous results in image generation. However,
due to the iterative nature of the diffusion process and its reliance on
classifier-free guidance, inference times are slow. In this paper, we propose a
new distillation approach for guided diffusion models in which an external
lightweight guide model is trained while the original text-to-image model
remains frozen. We show that our method reduces the inference computation of
classifier-free guided latent-space diffusion models by almost half, and only
requires 1\% trainable parameters of the base model. Furthermore, once trained,
our guide model can be applied to various fine-tuned, domain-specific versions
of the base diffusion model without the need for additional training: this
"plug-and-play" functionality drastically improves inference computation while
maintaining the visual fidelity of generated images. Empirically, we show that
our approach is able to produce visually appealing results and achieve a
comparable FID score to the teacher with as few as 8 to 16 steps.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.01954v2.pdf},
 author = {Yi-Ting Hsiao and Siavash Khodadadeh and Kevin Duarte and Wei-An Lin and Hui Qu and Mingi Kwon and Ratheesh Kalarot},
 title = {Plug-and-Play Diffusion Distillation},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{huang-2024-reverse,
 abstract = {To generate data from trained diffusion models, most inference algorithms,
such as DDPM, DDIM, and other variants, rely on discretizing the reverse SDEs
or their equivalent ODEs. In this paper, we view such approaches as decomposing
the entire denoising diffusion process into several segments, each
corresponding to a reverse transition kernel (RTK) sampling subproblem.
Specifically, DDPM uses a Gaussian approximation for the RTK, resulting in low
per-subproblem complexity but requiring a large number of segments (i.e.,
subproblems), which is conjectured to be inefficient. To address this, we
develop a general RTK framework that enables a more balanced subproblem
decomposition, resulting in $\tilde O(1)$ subproblems, each with strongly
log-concave targets. We then propose leveraging two fast sampling algorithms,
the Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm (MALA) and Underdamped Langevin
Dynamics (ULD), for solving these strongly log-concave subproblems. This gives
rise to the RTK-MALA and RTK-ULD algorithms for diffusion inference. In theory,
we further develop the convergence guarantees for RTK-MALA and RTK-ULD in total
variation (TV) distance: RTK-ULD can achieve $\epsilon$ target error within
$\tilde{\mathcal O}(d^{1/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ under mild conditions, and RTK-MALA
enjoys a $\mathcal{O}(d^{2}\log(d/\epsilon))$ convergence rate under slightly
stricter conditions. These theoretical results surpass the state-of-the-art
convergence rates for diffusion inference and are well supported by numerical
experiments.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16387v1.pdf},
 author = {Xunpeng Huang and Difan Zou and Hanze Dong and Yi Zhang and Yi-An Ma and Tong Zhang},
 title = {Reverse Transition Kernel: A Flexible Framework to Accelerate Diffusion Inference},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{kim-2024-pagoda,
 abstract = {The diffusion model performs remarkable in generating high-dimensional
content but is computationally intensive, especially during training. We
propose Progressive Growing of Diffusion Autoencoder (PaGoDA), a novel pipeline
that reduces the training costs through three stages: training diffusion on
downsampled data, distilling the pretrained diffusion, and progressive
super-resolution. With the proposed pipeline, PaGoDA achieves a $64\times$
reduced cost in training its diffusion model on 8x downsampled data; while at
the inference, with the single-step, it performs state-of-the-art on ImageNet
across all resolutions from 64x64 to 512x512, and text-to-image. PaGoDA's
pipeline can be applied directly in the latent space, adding compression
alongside the pre-trained autoencoder in Latent Diffusion Models (e.g., Stable
Diffusion). The code is available at https://github.com/sony/pagoda.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.14822v2.pdf},
 author = {Dongjun Kim and Chieh-Hsin Lai and Wei-Hsiang Liao and Yuhta Takida and Naoki Murata and Toshimitsu Uesaka and Yuki Mitsufuji and Stefano Ermon},
 github_url = {https://github.com/sony/pagoda},
 title = {PaGoDA: Progressive Growing of a One-Step Generator from a Low-Resolution Diffusion Teacher},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{li-2023-faster,
 abstract = {One of the main drawback of diffusion models is the slow inference time for
image generation. Among the most successful approaches to addressing this
problem are distillation methods. However, these methods require considerable
computational resources. In this paper, we take another approach to diffusion
model acceleration. We conduct a comprehensive study of the UNet encoder and
empirically analyze the encoder features. This provides insights regarding
their changes during the inference process. In particular, we find that encoder
features change minimally, whereas the decoder features exhibit substantial
variations across different time-steps. This insight motivates us to omit
encoder computation at certain adjacent time-steps and reuse encoder features
of previous time-steps as input to the decoder in multiple time-steps.
Importantly, this allows us to perform decoder computation in parallel, further
accelerating the denoising process. Additionally, we introduce a prior noise
injection method to improve the texture details in the generated image. Besides
the standard text-to-image task, we also validate our approach on other tasks:
text-to-video, personalized generation and reference-guided generation. Without
utilizing any knowledge distillation technique, our approach accelerates both
the Stable Diffusion (SD) and DeepFloyd-IF model sampling by 41$\%$ and 24$\%$
respectively, and DiT model sampling by 34$\%$, while maintaining high-quality
generation performance.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.09608v2.pdf},
 author = {Senmao Li and Taihang Hu and Joost van de Weijer and Fahad Shahbaz Khan and Tao Liu and Linxuan Li and Shiqi Yang and Yaxing Wang and Ming-Ming Cheng and Jian Yang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/dbolya/tomesd},
 title = {Faster Diffusion: Rethinking the Role of the Encoder for Diffusion Model Inference},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{li-2023-snapfusion,
 abstract = {Text-to-image diffusion models can create stunning images from natural
language descriptions that rival the work of professional artists and
photographers. However, these models are large, with complex network
architectures and tens of denoising iterations, making them computationally
expensive and slow to run. As a result, high-end GPUs and cloud-based inference
are required to run diffusion models at scale. This is costly and has privacy
implications, especially when user data is sent to a third party. To overcome
these challenges, we present a generic approach that, for the first time,
unlocks running text-to-image diffusion models on mobile devices in less than
$2$ seconds. We achieve so by introducing efficient network architecture and
improving step distillation. Specifically, we propose an efficient UNet by
identifying the redundancy of the original model and reducing the computation
of the image decoder via data distillation. Further, we enhance the step
distillation by exploring training strategies and introducing regularization
from classifier-free guidance. Our extensive experiments on MS-COCO show that
our model with $8$ denoising steps achieves better FID and CLIP scores than
Stable Diffusion v$1.5$ with $50$ steps. Our work democratizes content creation
by bringing powerful text-to-image diffusion models to the hands of users.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00980v3.pdf},
 author = {Yanyu Li and Huan Wang and Qing Jin and Ju Hu and Pavlo Chemerys and Yun Fu and Yanzhi Wang and Sergey Tulyakov and Jian Ren},
 github_url = {https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers},
 title = {SnapFusion: Text-to-Image Diffusion Model on Mobile Devices within Two Seconds},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{meng-2022-distillation,
 abstract = {Classifier-free guided diffusion models have recently been shown to be highly
effective at high-resolution image generation, and they have been widely used
in large-scale diffusion frameworks including DALLE-2, Stable Diffusion and
Imagen. However, a downside of classifier-free guided diffusion models is that
they are computationally expensive at inference time since they require
evaluating two diffusion models, a class-conditional model and an unconditional
model, tens to hundreds of times. To deal with this limitation, we propose an
approach to distilling classifier-free guided diffusion models into models that
are fast to sample from: Given a pre-trained classifier-free guided model, we
first learn a single model to match the output of the combined conditional and
unconditional models, and then we progressively distill that model to a
diffusion model that requires much fewer sampling steps. For standard diffusion
models trained on the pixel-space, our approach is able to generate images
visually comparable to that of the original model using as few as 4 sampling
steps on ImageNet 64x64 and CIFAR-10, achieving FID/IS scores comparable to
that of the original model while being up to 256 times faster to sample from.
For diffusion models trained on the latent-space (e.g., Stable Diffusion), our
approach is able to generate high-fidelity images using as few as 1 to 4
denoising steps, accelerating inference by at least 10-fold compared to
existing methods on ImageNet 256x256 and LAION datasets. We further demonstrate
the effectiveness of our approach on text-guided image editing and inpainting,
where our distilled model is able to generate high-quality results using as few
as 2-4 denoising steps.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03142v3.pdf},
 author = {Chenlin Meng and Robin Rombach and Ruiqi Gao and Diederik P. Kingma and Stefano Ermon and Jonathan Ho and Tim Salimans},
 github_url = {https://github.com/CompVis/stable-diffusion},
 title = {On Distillation of Guided Diffusion Models},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{moon-2024-simple,
 abstract = {Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance in generation problems
over various domains including images, videos, text, and audio. A practical
bottleneck of diffusion models is their sampling speed, due to the repeated
evaluation of score estimation networks during the inference. In this work, we
propose a novel framework capable of adaptively allocating compute required for
the score estimation, thereby reducing the overall sampling time of diffusion
models. We observe that the amount of computation required for the score
estimation may vary along the time step for which the score is estimated. Based
on this observation, we propose an early-exiting scheme, where we skip the
subset of parameters in the score estimation network during the inference,
based on a time-dependent exit schedule. Using the diffusion models for image
synthesis, we show that our method could significantly improve the sampling
throughput of the diffusion models without compromising image quality.
Furthermore, we also demonstrate that our method seamlessly integrates with
various types of solvers for faster sampling, capitalizing on their
compatibility to enhance overall efficiency. The source code and our
experiments are available at \url{https://github.com/taehong-moon/ee-diffusion}},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.05927v1.pdf},
 author = {Taehong Moon and Moonseok Choi and EungGu Yun and Jongmin Yoon and Gayoung Lee and Jaewoong Cho and Juho Lee},
 title = {A Simple Early Exiting Framework for Accelerated Sampling in Diffusion Models},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{phung-2022-wavelet,
 abstract = {Diffusion models are rising as a powerful solution for high-fidelity image
generation, which exceeds GANs in quality in many circumstances. However, their
slow training and inference speed is a huge bottleneck, blocking them from
being used in real-time applications. A recent DiffusionGAN method
significantly decreases the models' running time by reducing the number of
sampling steps from thousands to several, but their speeds still largely lag
behind the GAN counterparts. This paper aims to reduce the speed gap by
proposing a novel wavelet-based diffusion scheme. We extract low-and-high
frequency components from both image and feature levels via wavelet
decomposition and adaptively handle these components for faster processing
while maintaining good generation quality. Furthermore, we propose to use a
reconstruction term, which effectively boosts the model training convergence.
Experimental results on CelebA-HQ, CIFAR-10, LSUN-Church, and STL-10 datasets
prove our solution is a stepping-stone to offering real-time and high-fidelity
diffusion models. Our code and pre-trained checkpoints are available at
\url{https://github.com/VinAIResearch/WaveDiff.git}.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.16152v2.pdf},
 author = {Hao Phung and Quan Dao and Anh Tran},
 title = {Wavelet Diffusion Models Are Fast and Scalable Image Generators},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{salimans-2024-multistep,
 abstract = {We present a new method for making diffusion models faster to sample. The
method distills many-step diffusion models into few-step models by matching
conditional expectations of the clean data given noisy data along the sampling
trajectory. Our approach extends recently proposed one-step methods to the
multi-step case, and provides a new perspective by interpreting these
approaches in terms of moment matching. By using up to 8 sampling steps, we
obtain distilled models that outperform not only their one-step versions but
also their original many-step teacher models, obtaining new state-of-the-art
results on the Imagenet dataset. We also show promising results on a large
text-to-image model where we achieve fast generation of high resolution images
directly in image space, without needing autoencoders or upsamplers.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.04103v1.pdf},
 author = {Tim Salimans and Thomas Mensink and Jonathan Heek and Emiel Hoogeboom},
 github_url = {https://github.com/google/jax},
 title = {Multistep Distillation of Diffusion Models via Moment Matching},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{shang-2022-post,
 abstract = {Denoising diffusion (score-based) generative models have recently achieved
significant accomplishments in generating realistic and diverse data. These
approaches define a forward diffusion process for transforming data into noise
and a backward denoising process for sampling data from noise. Unfortunately,
the generation process of current denoising diffusion models is notoriously
slow due to the lengthy iterative noise estimations, which rely on cumbersome
neural networks. It prevents the diffusion models from being widely deployed,
especially on edge devices. Previous works accelerate the generation process of
diffusion model (DM) via finding shorter yet effective sampling trajectories.
However, they overlook the cost of noise estimation with a heavy network in
every iteration. In this work, we accelerate generation from the perspective of
compressing the noise estimation network. Due to the difficulty of retraining
DMs, we exclude mainstream training-aware compression paradigms and introduce
post-training quantization (PTQ) into DM acceleration. However, the output
distributions of noise estimation networks change with time-step, making
previous PTQ methods fail in DMs since they are designed for single-time step
scenarios. To devise a DM-specific PTQ method, we explore PTQ on DM in three
aspects: quantized operations, calibration dataset, and calibration metric. We
summarize and use several observations derived from all-inclusive
investigations to formulate our method, which especially targets the unique
multi-time-step structure of DMs. Experimentally, our method can directly
quantize full-precision DMs into 8-bit models while maintaining or even
improving their performance in a training-free manner. Importantly, our method
can serve as a plug-and-play module on other fast-sampling methods, e.g., DDIM.
The code is available at https://github.com/42Shawn/PTQ4DM .},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.15736v3.pdf},
 author = {Yuzhang Shang and Zhihang Yuan and Bin Xie and Bingzhe Wu and Yan Yan},
 github_url = {https://github.com/42Shawn/PTQ4DM},
 title = {Post-Training Quantization on Diffusion Models},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{so-2023-temporal,
 abstract = {The diffusion model has gained popularity in vision applications due to its
remarkable generative performance and versatility. However, high storage and
computation demands, resulting from the model size and iterative generation,
hinder its use on mobile devices. Existing quantization techniques struggle to
maintain performance even in 8-bit precision due to the diffusion model's
unique property of temporal variation in activation. We introduce a novel
quantization method that dynamically adjusts the quantization interval based on
time step information, significantly improving output quality. Unlike
conventional dynamic quantization techniques, our approach has no computational
overhead during inference and is compatible with both post-training
quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT). Our extensive
experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in output quality with the
quantized diffusion model across various datasets.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.02316v2.pdf},
 author = {Junhyuk So and Jungwon Lee and Daehyun Ahn and Hyungjun Kim and Eunhyeok Park},
 title = {Temporal Dynamic Quantization for Diffusion Models},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{wizadwongsa-2023-accelerating,
 abstract = {Guided diffusion is a technique for conditioning the output of a diffusion
model at sampling time without retraining the network for each specific task.
One drawback of diffusion models, however, is their slow sampling process.
Recent techniques can accelerate unguided sampling by applying high-order
numerical methods to the sampling process when viewed as differential
equations. On the contrary, we discover that the same techniques do not work
for guided sampling, and little has been explored about its acceleration. This
paper explores the culprit of this problem and provides a solution based on
operator splitting methods, motivated by our key finding that classical
high-order numerical methods are unsuitable for the conditional function. Our
proposed method can re-utilize the high-order methods for guided sampling and
can generate images with the same quality as a 250-step DDIM baseline using
32-58% less sampling time on ImageNet256. We also demonstrate usage on a wide
variety of conditional generation tasks, such as text-to-image generation,
colorization, inpainting, and super-resolution.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.11558v1.pdf},
 author = {Suttisak Wizadwongsa and Supasorn Suwajanakorn},
 github_url = {https://github.com/sWizad/split-diffusion},
 title = {Accelerating Guided Diffusion Sampling with Splitting Numerical Methods},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{wizadwongsa-2023-diffusion,
 abstract = {Despite the remarkable success of diffusion models in image generation, slow
sampling remains a persistent issue. To accelerate the sampling process, prior
studies have reformulated diffusion sampling as an ODE/SDE and introduced
higher-order numerical methods. However, these methods often produce divergence
artifacts, especially with a low number of sampling steps, which limits the
achievable acceleration. In this paper, we investigate the potential causes of
these artifacts and suggest that the small stability regions of these methods
could be the principal cause. To address this issue, we propose two novel
techniques. The first technique involves the incorporation of Heavy Ball (HB)
momentum, a well-known technique for improving optimization, into existing
diffusion numerical methods to expand their stability regions. We also prove
that the resulting methods have first-order convergence. The second technique,
called Generalized Heavy Ball (GHVB), constructs a new high-order method that
offers a variable trade-off between accuracy and artifact suppression.
Experimental results show that our techniques are highly effective in reducing
artifacts and improving image quality, surpassing state-of-the-art diffusion
solvers on both pixel-based and latent-based diffusion models for low-step
sampling. Our research provides novel insights into the design of numerical
methods for future diffusion work.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.11118v1.pdf},
 author = {Suttisak Wizadwongsa and Worameth Chinchuthakun and Pramook Khungurn and Amit Raj and Supasorn Suwajanakorn},
 github_url = {https://github.com/LuChengTHU/dpm-solver},
 title = {Diffusion Sampling with Momentum for Mitigating Divergence Artifacts},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{xu-2023-semi,
 abstract = {Despite the proliferation of generative models, achieving fast sampling
during inference without compromising sample diversity and quality remains
challenging. Existing models such as Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
(DDPM) deliver high-quality, diverse samples but are slowed by an inherently
high number of iterative steps. The Denoising Diffusion Generative Adversarial
Networks (DDGAN) attempted to circumvent this limitation by integrating a GAN
model for larger jumps in the diffusion process. However, DDGAN encountered
scalability limitations when applied to large datasets. To address these
limitations, we introduce a novel approach that tackles the problem by matching
implicit and explicit factors. More specifically, our approach involves
utilizing an implicit model to match the marginal distributions of noisy data
and the explicit conditional distribution of the forward diffusion. This
combination allows us to effectively match the joint denoising distributions.
Unlike DDPM but similar to DDGAN, we do not enforce a parametric distribution
for the reverse step, enabling us to take large steps during inference. Similar
to the DDPM but unlike DDGAN, we take advantage of the exact form of the
diffusion process. We demonstrate that our proposed method obtains comparable
generative performance to diffusion-based models and vastly superior results to
models with a small number of sampling steps.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12511v3.pdf},
 author = {Yanwu Xu and Mingming Gong and Shaoan Xie and Wei Wei and Matthias Grundmann and Kayhan Batmanghelich and Tingbo Hou},
 title = {Semi-Implicit Denoising Diffusion Models (SIDDMs)},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{xue-2024-accelerating,
 abstract = {Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have shown remarkable performance in
high-resolution image synthesis, but their sampling efficiency is still to be
desired due to the typically large number of sampling steps. Recent
advancements in high-order numerical ODE solvers for DPMs have enabled the
generation of high-quality images with much fewer sampling steps. While this is
a significant development, most sampling methods still employ uniform time
steps, which is not optimal when using a small number of steps. To address this
issue, we propose a general framework for designing an optimization problem
that seeks more appropriate time steps for a specific numerical ODE solver for
DPMs. This optimization problem aims to minimize the distance between the
ground-truth solution to the ODE and an approximate solution corresponding to
the numerical solver. It can be efficiently solved using the constrained trust
region method, taking less than $15$ seconds. Our extensive experiments on both
unconditional and conditional sampling using pixel- and latent-space DPMs
demonstrate that, when combined with the state-of-the-art sampling method
UniPC, our optimized time steps significantly improve image generation
performance in terms of FID scores for datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet,
compared to using uniform time steps.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.17376v3.pdf},
 author = {Shuchen Xue and Zhaoqiang Liu and Fei Chen and Shifeng Zhang and Tianyang Hu and Enze Xie and Zhenguo Li},
 title = {Accelerating Diffusion Sampling with Optimized Time Steps},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{ye-2024-training,
 abstract = {Diffusion models have recently achieved great success in the synthesis of
high-quality images and videos. However, the existing denoising techniques in
diffusion models are commonly based on step-by-step noise predictions, which
suffers from high computation cost, resulting in a prohibitive latency for
interactive applications. In this paper, we propose AdaptiveDiffusion to
relieve this bottleneck by adaptively reducing the noise prediction steps
during the denoising process. Our method considers the potential of skipping as
many noise prediction steps as possible while keeping the final denoised
results identical to the original full-step ones. Specifically, the skipping
strategy is guided by the third-order latent difference that indicates the
stability between timesteps during the denoising process, which benefits the
reusing of previous noise prediction results. Extensive experiments on image
and video diffusion models demonstrate that our method can significantly speed
up the denoising process while generating identical results to the original
process, achieving up to an average 2~5x speedup without quality degradation.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.09873v1.pdf},
 author = {Hancheng Ye and Jiakang Yuan and Renqiu Xia and Xiangchao Yan and Tao Chen and Junchi Yan and Botian Shi and Bo Zhang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/horseee/DeepCache},
 title = {Training-Free Adaptive Diffusion with Bounded Difference Approximation Strategy},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{zhou-2023-fast,
 abstract = {Sampling from diffusion models can be treated as solving the corresponding
ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with the aim of obtaining an accurate
solution with as few number of function evaluations (NFE) as possible.
Recently, various fast samplers utilizing higher-order ODE solvers have emerged
and achieved better performance than the initial first-order one. However,
these numerical methods inherently result in certain approximation errors,
which significantly degrades sample quality with extremely small NFE (e.g.,
around 5). In contrast, based on the geometric observation that each sampling
trajectory almost lies in a two-dimensional subspace embedded in the ambient
space, we propose Approximate MEan-Direction Solver (AMED-Solver) that
eliminates truncation errors by directly learning the mean direction for fast
diffusion sampling. Besides, our method can be easily used as a plugin to
further improve existing ODE-based samplers. Extensive experiments on image
synthesis with the resolution ranging from 32 to 512 demonstrate the
effectiveness of our method. With only 5 NFE, we achieve 6.61 FID on CIFAR-10,
10.74 FID on ImageNet 64$\times$64, and 13.20 FID on LSUN Bedroom. Our code is
available at https://github.com/zju-pi/diff-sampler.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.00094v3.pdf},
 author = {Zhenyu Zhou and Defang Chen and Can Wang and Chun Chen},
 title = {Fast ODE-based Sampling for Diffusion Models in Around 5 Steps},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{ho-2022-classifier,
 abstract = {Classifier guidance is a recently introduced method to trade off mode
coverage and sample fidelity in conditional diffusion models post training, in
the same spirit as low temperature sampling or truncation in other types of
generative models. Classifier guidance combines the score estimate of a
diffusion model with the gradient of an image classifier and thereby requires
training an image classifier separate from the diffusion model. It also raises
the question of whether guidance can be performed without a classifier. We show
that guidance can be indeed performed by a pure generative model without such a
classifier: in what we call classifier-free guidance, we jointly train a
conditional and an unconditional diffusion model, and we combine the resulting
conditional and unconditional score estimates to attain a trade-off between
sample quality and diversity similar to that obtained using classifier
guidance.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598v1.pdf},
 author = {Jonathan Ho and Tim Salimans},
 title = {Classifier-free diffusion guidance},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{kingma-2023-understanding,
 abstract = {To achieve the highest perceptual quality, state-of-the-art diffusion models
are optimized with objectives that typically look very different from the
maximum likelihood and the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) objectives. In this
work, we reveal that diffusion model objectives are actually closely related to
the ELBO.
  Specifically, we show that all commonly used diffusion model objectives
equate to a weighted integral of ELBOs over different noise levels, where the
weighting depends on the specific objective used. Under the condition of
monotonic weighting, the connection is even closer: the diffusion objective
then equals the ELBO, combined with simple data augmentation, namely Gaussian
noise perturbation. We show that this condition holds for a number of
state-of-the-art diffusion models.
  In experiments, we explore new monotonic weightings and demonstrate their
effectiveness, achieving state-of-the-art FID scores on the high-resolution
ImageNet benchmark.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.00848v7.pdf},
 author = {Diederik P. Kingma and Ruiqi Gao},
 title = {Understanding the diffusion objective as a weighted integral of elbos},
 year = {2023}
}
